speechtext:
Since last fall
the colonization departments of the two railroads, instead of directing their efforts towards securing the entry of new migrants into Canada have, at the instance of the government, joined their colonization forces with the forces of the department over which I am presiding with a view to placing as many unemployed as possible who are now in the cities, on the farm or in other useful occupations. We have heard, and I have listened to many statements in the house, about the dire conditions alleged to exist on the farms all over Canada. In spite of that, this effort prior to the end of last month has resulted in some 7,600 single unemployed men being placed with the farmers of this country, and very few of them have returned to the cities.
In addition to that we have been able, with the joint help of the railroads and my department, to place on selected locations some 1,500 families who have been paddling their

own canoe, as it were, and have established themselves on the farm. I have no record, nor has our department, nor have the railroads, of one of those families coming back to the city to join the ranks of the unemployed. With a view to furthering that work and to consolidating the efforts of all those who have been heretofore engaged in bringing migrants into Canada, a conference is being held in Winnipeg and another, I hope, will be held in the east. Wherever my department can find in the various localities places in which unemployment can be relieved in this way, this work is being carried on without any expense to the government other than that of maintaining the ordinary staff.

The house resumed from Monday, June 8, consideration in committee of Bill No. 4, to amend the Copyright Act-Mr. Cahan-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 10-Performing rights.

Last evening the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) in answer to a question that was put to him by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) and replying also to a question which I had asked, said, as reported at page 2415 of Hansard:
Allow me to answer the question. Article 4, clause 2, of the convention, provides that the extent of protection as well as the means of redress to safeguard the rights of authors shall be governed exclusively by the laws of the country whose protection is claimed.
But the hon. gentleman forgot to read a little further. Article 4 of the convention of Berne, as it appears on page 8 of the printed bill now under review, adds these words, "apart from the express stipulations of the present convention." That is, the Canadian parliament may enact any means of redress provided that the Canadian law has previously complied with the express stipulations of the Berne convention, to which convention Canada is a contracting party, and by the terms of which Canada is bound to provide the means of redress and which this bill fails to enact.
The hon. minister also, at page 2410 of Hansard, said this:
But this I do say-that the public opinion of this country -is very close to this stage, that if certain regulations which we propose
to enact in this bill are not within the Berne convention, then public opinion in this country is in such a state that the great body of it may say that the sooner Canada gets out of the Berne convention, the better for Canada.
Now if public opinion in Canada is so strong as to force the Canadian parliament to legalize the spoliation of authors' rights, of the rights of nationals and of the rights of the unionists, in contravention of the terms of the convention of Berne, and if the present legislation is the result of that public opinion, then I say that it is incumbent upon the minister to propose the immediate withdrawal of Canada from the Berne convention, and from my seat now I challenge the minister to do it.
I do not intend, Mr. Chairman, to rehash the debate of last evening. We are now on section 10, and I propose to discuss it.
That permeates the whole of the hon. gentleman's speech, and I wanted to answer.
The hon. gentleman should have answered when the clause in question was under discussion.

Shortly after 1886 something rather similar happened. Sir John Thompson went over to Europe to protest against the admission of Canada into the Berne convention, and he did that because there were certain interests in Canada that forced him to do so.
We are on section 10, Mr. Chairman, and I think the hon. gentleman should confine his remarks to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect, my hon. friend should not discuss the principle of the bill at this stage. I would ask him to confine his remarks to a discussion of the clause before the committee.

I accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman, with the very best grace. I shall have an opportunity of coming to that question later.
Coming to clause 10, I would have very much preferred had it not been embodied in the bill at all. I do not think it is a proper section to be introduced in a copyright bill, and I suggested that before the committee. However, the committee thought otherwise, and its view prevailed. I think a lot of difficulty would have been obviated had this section found its place in a different statute, namely, in the Combines Investigation Act. My objection to this section is that it is in
Copyright, Act

flagrant contradiction of the Berne convention. Obviously, and I think the hon. minister did not intend to hide this in any way, this section is directed against what is called a certain performing right society. It is, I think, well within the understanding of every member of this committee that authors cannot themselves the world over look after their own interests, that there must 'be in Canada for the authors of France, Germany, Japan and the forty odd nations o-f the world, some body that will look after their interests, just as there must be in those other countries some body that will look after the interests of Canadian authors there. It is true, as the hon. gentleman has said, that this company represents some .thirty thousand authors, but where I take issue with the hon, gentleman is as to the nature of the assignment which he invokes when he says that we are not legislating by this clause against the authors, 'but against some body that is absolutely new .because of the nature of the assignment that has taken place. The hon. gentleman, I think, limited his remarks to the two factions in .conflict in this peculiar situation, namely, the Performing Right Society and the users of music. I desire to place before this committee the situation in its true light as it was placed before the committee of which I had the honour of being a member. I think it is only fair that this committee should see just what are the two influences at work, for the public at no time was represented before the committee. The public was not at stake. I't was clearly a question between the Performing Right Society, holding certain assigned rights of the authors, and those who endeavoured to use those rights. When the author assigns his rights, performing rights or musical rights, he is not vesting his total 100 per cent of his rights in these societies. He simply turns over his rights to these associations or societies or companies for the punpose of having his fees and royalties collected. I want to refer to the evidence of these two conflicting interests, given before the special committee. At page 81 of the evidence Mr. John A. Cooper was called and sworn, and I want to place his evidence before this committee so that hon. members may see juSt whom we are trying to protect and whose interests are at stake. I quote from the evidence:
John A. Cooper, called and sworn.
By the Chairman:
Q. Please give us your name, residence and occupation.-A. I am president of the Motion Picture Distributors and Exhibitors Association of Canada. My address is 53 Binscarth road, Toronto. I am also, to-day, sir, if I may be allowed, representing the Province of Quebec Theatre Owners' Association, which com-
prises most of the theatre owners of the province of Quebec, the independent theatre owners of the province of Ontario, the Motion Picture Association of the Province of Manitoba, and the Saskatchewan Independent Theatre Owners, and a certain number of theatre owners in the other provinces who are not formed into an association. I would like to point out, sir, if I may, that these combined people whom I represent have nearly one hundred million dollars invested in this country, and that they employ somewhere around fifteen thousand people, so that I have to be careful in representing such large interests. Will it be necessary to say anything about the Motion Picture Association-the main association that I represent?
Q. We will leave that to your discretion?- A. I will be very glad to say what this association represents. It represents ten of twelve distributors of motion pictures in Canada, including the Famous Lasky Film Service, Regal Films Limited, Fox Films Corporation, Canadian Universal Film Company, Canadian Educational Films, United Artists Association, Mary Pickford's Company, Warner Brothers Pictures, the First National, and Columbia Pictures. These companies distribute practically all the pictures that are distributed in Canada, whether those pictures are made in England, Germany, France or the United States. Our association is not an association for profit,-
Oh!
-but merely an association such as the Canadian Manufacturers Association, to take care of matters of general interest to all these companies, and these companies are, in fact, highly organized competitors for the business of distributing motion pictures to the thousand theatres from coast to coast.
There is not one word in that evidence about looking after the interests of the public in any way, shape or form, whatsoever. The association is formed simply for the purpose of looking after the distribution of motion pictures to the thousands of theatres from coast to coast. If ever there was a monopoly to which the minister should direct his attention, that is one. So that we may view the other side of the medal, because I have never seen a medal without two sides, let us see what the Canadian Performing Right Society is. At page 4 of the evidence heard before the committee Mr. Henry T. Jamieson was called and sworn, and I shall read from his evidence:
I am president of the Canadian Performing Right Society residing in Toronto.
At a later point in his evidence I find the following:
The Canadian Performing Right Society, Limited, was duly incorporated in 1925, under the provisions of the first part of chapter 79, of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, known as "The Companies Act," and amending acts.
Here is a Canadian company, and because it happens to be a Canadian company is it

Copyright Act
going to be singled out? The other conflicting interests are not incorporated in Canada. Mr. Cooper does not mention any of them, and therefore we have difficulty in following their operations. Then Mr. Jamieson goes on to say:
The society was formed as a branch of The Performing Right Society, Limited, of London, England, and, since 1930, has been jointly operated by that society and the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers.
The British and American societies are associations of composers, authors, -publishers and proprietors of copyright musical works, established to collect fees for the public performance of such works and to restrain unauthorized performances thereof. Through these societies, the Canadian society controls the Canadian performing rights in the works owned by the members of the British and American societies and of the kindred societies in France. Germany, Austria, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Roumania, Denmark, Hungary, Poland, Switzerland, Czechoslovakia, Portugal and Brazil. Norway and Finland, affiliated with the British society.
The Canadian rights, owned by the members of all the societies mentioned, are obtained under the Canadian Copyright Act, 1921. This follows the International Copyright Convention of Berne as revised at Berlin in 1908, to which Canada adhered on 1st January, 1924.
Then I pass on to page 5, and read the third paragraph on the page:
The Canadian Performing Right Society, Limited, is the organization formed for the purpose of collecting fees in this country for the public performances of Canadian, British or foreign musical works, in which copyright subsists under the Canadian act.
From the same page I shall now quote paragraph (3):
(3) Aims and objects of Canadian society:
Members, as distinct from licence holders, on election invest the societies with sole authority to grant licences in the several countries mentioned, to collect fees in respect of public performances of their copyright musical works and, on their behalf, to exercise and enforce all rights and remedies relating thereto.
The Canadian society represents 917 British authors and composers, 102 British publishers, 711 American authors and composers, 91 American publishers and 26,500 members of the affiliated foreign societies.
In all, about 30,000 authors.
Both the controlling societies are membership societies. These societies are directed by the members (authors, composers and publishers). No membership fees are paid. No dividends are paid.
Now the stage is set. Those are the two interests in conflict. Not a single word has been given in evidence to the effect that at any time the Performing Right Society had been guilty of a hold up or had refused, after offer of a reasonable sum, to grant a licence to any one applying. Undoubtedly it might
not be unwise for the government to have control over certain societies which owe their existence to statutory enactments. The evidence in committee-and I am going by that evidence-did not disclose any reason to impose this legislation. We are simply anticipating a situation which may never arise. At all events present conditions do not at all indicate that a situation requiring such legislation will arise in the near future. It might be said that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. I think, however, it would be wiser to wait until an occasion arises which would necessitate the investigation or regulation of this company. I wish that every member of this committee might be privileged to read the most able and fair presentation of the argument on behalf of this society made by Mr. Anglin, KU, of Toronto. I think the purpose would be eminently served if hon. members would avail themselves of the first opportunity of reading the argument.
I shall now refer to subsection (a) of section 10 of the bill. In conformity with this section all lists of titles in respect of which fees will be charged, must be filed. In that connection I wish to refer to the evidence given by Mr. Howard Angus Kennedy, and for that purpose I refer to page 116 of the evidence. After being sworn Mr. Kennedy, when asked his occupation, said:
I was going to say I appear both as a writer and as a farmer. You can put that down, it is quite true. At the present time, not having to depend on my farm, I hope, I am national secretary of the Canadian Authors' Association, an association which. I suppose I should explain, consists of 850 members, in 12 branches, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia -besides an entirely French section in the province of Quebec.
The association was formed ten years ago, largely to promote and to obtain a just copyright act for the dominion, although for other purposes also. Speaking for myself, just as a joke, when I said I was a farmer, I am a farmer in Mr. Irvine's constituency of Wetas-kiwin, and not altogether independent of agriculture either. But I am also an author. I have been writing very largely for the benefit of Canada. I do not claim remuneration or particular credit for that, but, for the last fifty years, and it is just fifty years last week since I became a writer in Canada-I have devoted myself very largely to Canadian subjects and also, very largely, to the spreading of knowledge and appreciation of Canada in other countries. especially in the old country, Great Britain and Ireland.
I have quoted that section of the evidence so that hon. members may know who Mr. Kennedy is. Then, to quote from page 117 of the evidence:
I should say that it seems to me, sir, that the amendments to the bill, especially sections 1C and 11-
Copyright Act

Which are now incorporated in section 6.
-that have been spoken so much about, would allow those who have no respect for the Berne convention, as you have, sir, and do not care cue snap about it, to drive a coach and four through it. That, we are deeply concerned with preventing, but we are also concerned with other things-we are local people; we are Canadian people-I have got a book here, one of my books to which a sequel has just been written-I have just got the plates. It is a book of stories. I have been asked to turn some of those stories into musical plays for children. I will at once come under two of the sections of this bill. I would be practically compelled, if I did so and wanted to get anything out of it, to put my interests in the hands of the Performing Right Society, Mr. Thompson's new society, or our own association, which might quite conceivably branch out into those lines and take the interests of those musical numbers in charge, and would immediately be one of the associations against which your section 10 is aimed.
He would therefore find that his royalties and fees would be limited by order in council. Then he says:
We are to be subject to price fixing, and we ask why we should be discriminated against, and why should you not subject to price fixing your butcher, baker or candlestick maker, your theatre, your dealer, everybody?
I spoke of myself as a farmer. I am interested in wheat. The question of price-fixing is constantly coming up in relation to wheat. You had the fixing of price during the war to a maximum beyond which we should not go.
Without introducing politics at all, as was agreed, may I say I have heard the right hon. Prime Minister declare that there was to be no price fixing in the matter of which I have just spoken.
Does my hon. friend think it fair to make a comparison between wheat and copyright in this regard?

One is a necessity, the other is a luxury. No one needs a luxury for his livelihood, and if anyone wants to have it he must pay a fair price for it; whereas wheat being a necessity might be subject to regulation.
But the price the farmer gets for his wheat does not depend on a statute, while the only right the author has, -his copyright-is established by this parliament.
I am not saying it in any unkindly spirit, but if my hon. friend is satisfied with the distinction, well and good.
Certainly the remark is very relevant.
If anyone wants to hold up the price of wheat or of bread, then parliament has the right of investigation and-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I suggest if the hon. gentleman wishes to discuss this clause that he direct his attention to it. We are not discussing the price of wheat; it is not part of this bill. The evidence the hon. gentleman has cited is printed and in the hands of all members, and undoubtedly those who are interested in the question have read that evidence. Why should there be this obstruction? Why should we discuss the bill in this irrelevant manner? I suggest that the hon. gentleman direct his remarks to section 10 and allow us to discuss it.
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) will admit that I have done my very best to facilitate the passage of this bill.
Certainly.
I think it is quite in order for the member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) to quote the evidence.
I have no objection to his quoting the evidence so long as it is relevant to section 10.

The quotation was rather terse, but the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) put a question and the member for Ottawa, out of courtesy, was trying to reply. So I believe he is quite in order. I know the Secretary of State is very desirious to have this bill pass, and, I repeat, I share his desire, but I am sure he has not used the word "obstruction" with any desire to justify it.
Mr. CAHAN; I withdraw the word.

speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Ottawa has the right to make a comparison or analogy. I am not supposed to be very lenient in my rulings, bu't I think so far he is in order.
Mr. CHEVRIER; I am quite satisfied with your ruling, Mr. Chairman. Now I desire to quote a portion of Mr. Buck's evidence at page 36. I do so because I think it is the easiest way to enable us to reach a conclusion on this matter. It is only by establishing the facts and arguing on those facts that we can

Copyright Act
get somewhere. This evidence is on the question of fixing the price at which the licences will be issued. I am not making any legal argument on this, I am simply voicing the contentions of those whose rights are being so curtailed, namely, the authors. At page 36 Mr. Buck said:
Price fixing is a most dangerous and extraordinary subject. The gentlemen who utilize our works, namely, the motion picture owners, the radio broadcasters, the dance hall owners and those other gentlemen, are not subject to any regulations, and it takes a great deal of thought to wonder why the creator, the man who makes it possible for these things to exist, should be picked on when it comes down to regulations. There is no regulation to tell the broadcaster how much he should charge an hour; there is no regulation to tell the motion picture owner how much he should charge per seat, or how much he should put his picture on for, and through some peculiar trick of fate which I think is instigated by gentlemen loaded with a _ sinister purpose-and I wish to make the point, sir, that I am not here asking Canada for special favours, I am merely here trying to defend every Canadian author and composer.
That is the situation with reference to the parties in opposition to the amendment. This price fixing takes away from the author his inherent right to sell the product of his brain at the price which he wants to put upon it, or to retain his product if he does not want to sell it. True, the hon. gentleman throughout these proceedings will say that the author is not touched 'by this legislation, but that the assignee is. Well, copyright exists in the works defined in the statute during the lifetime of the author and fifty years after his death. The law is that that is an absolute, inherent right. It matters not into whose hands these works pass. I may go into a store and buy a book, but simply because I pay two dollars for the book, it does not mean that I have ithe right to alter the title, to distort the contents and to reprint the book under my naime and sell it. The character of copyright attaches to thie work itself for fifty years after the death of the author, no matter in what way the original owner may have disposed of his work. On this point I have the opinion of the British authorities contained in a letter from Lord Lovat, No. 356. It is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
Downing Street, 26 July, 1927.
Sir,-

The society known as the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited, which I think I referred to previously, by mistake, as the Performing Right Society of Canada Limited, is really a branch of the Performing Right Society, Limited, of London, England, and 22110-155
since 1930 has been jointly operated by the English Performing Right Society and the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers. The evidence did disclose that this Canadian company is organized under the Companies Act of Canada. Ten thousand shares are issued of no par value, five thousand of which are held by the American society, and five thousand by the English society. It is clearly in evidence that this society has not been able to function in Canada to the same extent as it has 'functioned in Great Britain by reason of the provisions of section 40 of our existing statute. They carried those provisions to the privy council seeking a construction favourable to the Canadian company in the Performing Right Society case, and the decision of the privy council was against them. We have modified section 40 of the existing act so as to remove every possible objection which has been urged by the Performing Right Society of England, the Performing Right Society of Canada or by the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers. Section 40 is now clear. However the provisions of the convention of Berne and the statutes which we have enacted in Canada to enable our courts to enforce the provisions of the Berne convention are all intended for the protection of authors, or in the case of musical works, composers who are authors within the meaning of the term. That convention and those statutes never contemplated the protection of a trading company, a combine or monopoly trading in the performing rights of authors which, to a large extent, it has purchased from those authors. At the convention at Berne and at the recent convention at Rome the position taken by the British delegates, so I am advised, was that there was nothing in either convention which would prevent any country, a member of the union, from enacting domestic legislation which would prevent abuses of monopolies created by combinations of individual authors. Therefore the legislation we now propose simply provides that in the future if this monopoly, which admittedly exists in Canada, should abuse its enormous powers to the injury and detriment of the Canadian people, if it should by its trading in these monopoly rights prove that its action and policy affect detrimentally the public interest, an inquiry shall be made into the facts and a report be made thereon for the consideration of the governor in council. There is nothing in this bill which takes away from the individual author or composer, or his assignee as such, the right to deal with his particular work. In this act every presumption is made in his favour. He comes into our courts as author and the presumption is

that if he asserts he is the author, then he is as a matter of fact such author, and is entitled to sue and recover damages. There is not one word in the bill now before the committee which prevents him recovering for either an infringement of the statute or for a recovery of fees, charges and royalties due to him in any action taken under his name.
However the moment we go beyond that and find about 30,000 or more authors, selling or parting with their interests in performing rights by assignments to this Canadian society to the extent that at the present time it holds a monopoly of 05 per cent of all modern music, so far as the territorial jurisdiction of Canada is concerned, such a monopoly if unregulated and unrestrained may, of its own option, create abuses in this country which would be utterly intolerable. For instance the society could decide that one theatre in a town may have a monopoly on modern music, and that the other theatre shall not have the advantage of performing rights in connection with any of these 3,000,000 works in respect of which the society controls such performing rights. The action of the society could ruin one of two hotels in any town where at the dinner hour music is given as entertainment. They could break one hotel by refusing to deal with it or to grant it performing rights, while to the competing hotel they could grant, for any sum they saw fit, performing rights in connection with those
3,000,000 works. It could do the same thing with regard to broadcasting companies. For instance, it may say to the Canadian Pacific Railway, "We will deal with you and give you exclusive broadcasting rights for 3,000,000 works," and on the other hand it may say to the Canadian National Railways "You shall not perform, at any price, any of those works." It can interfere with the whole theatrical business, the entire hotel business, and with public performance in every way of the musical works of which it has a monopoly. Those abuses, as they appear, must be dealt with. The section now under discussion, section 10, is framed merely for the purpose of providing a statutory warning to the monopoly to the effect that " If you do not deal justly, impartially and equitably with the Canadian public we will reserve the right to investigate you and to adopt certain remedial measures in respect of your abuses of your monopoly."

the House of Commons in England on July 3, 1930. The committee was composed of some of the most eminent men of the parliament of England and the report dealing with the Performing Right Society of England contains some clauses to which I shall now refer. In such circumstances, the fear of music users that the society	
The Performing Right Society of Great Britain.

Your committee are agreed that a fixed fee cannot be applied to all the varying circumstances of public performance if the composer is to receive a reasonable remuneration. Nor do they wish to place any obstacles in the way of composers forming an association for the purposes of protecting and enforcing their performing rights. Such an association is undoubtedly a convenience and almost a necessity, both to the composer, music publisher and the user of music who would be considerably embarrassed if he had to deal separately with each piece of music performed. In fact it may be said to be the only practicable way in which the composer can collect his fees for performing rights in any adequate manner.
The sentiments expressed in this report are those of good, English fair play. The report continues:

Your committee consider that such a supermonopoly can abuse its powers by refusing to grant licences upon reasonable terms so as to prejudice the trade or industry of persons carrying on business in this country and to be contrary to the public interest and that it should be open to those persons to obtain relief in respect of such abuse by appeal to arbitration or to some other tribunal. This should apply only in those cases where the ownership or control of copyright has been transferred to an association.
Section 10 of the bill now before the committee is framed on that basis. It simply provides that a society such as the Performing Right Society of Canada which is owned and controlled one-half by an American company and the other half by an English company, must come out in the open and file a list of the musical works in which it claims to have

Copyright Act
performing rights, and let the public know its fees, charges and royalties whether for individual works, or for all its works, en bloc. The public of Canada, which is now admittedly under the control of this widespread monopoly, asks that it give information by filing at a public office a list of its works and of its prices. The company is not attacked in any way, but if a complaint is made with respect to it there is a provision whereby the governor in council may order an inquiry and a report as to whether it-
-unduly withholds the issue or grant of licences for or in respect of the performance of such works in Canada, or proposes to collect excessive fees, charges or royalties in compensation for the issue or grant of such licences, or otherwise conducts its operations in Canada in a manner which is deemed detrimental to the interests of the public,-
Then on the report of the minister-the Secretary of State in this case-the governor in council may take action. It is not unique to suggest that the governor in council may take action, because under sectioil 13 of the present act, it is provided that the owner of the copyright in certain cases may be ordered to grant a licence to reproduce or perform the work in public, as the case may be, subject to such terms and to such conditions as the governor in council may think fit. Therefore the vesting in the governor in council of a certain authority in this matter is not introduced into the act for the first time; the amendment suggested in section 10 is entirely consistent and compatible with the provisions of the old act, which are not interfered with.	.
I am so anxious to see this bill out of committee that it may have an early hearing in another place that I do not wish to debate this section further unless some hon. member has further questions to ask me in regard to it.

I have tried to
find a definition of the term " dramatico-musical" used in this section, but without success, although I know the term is employed in the Berne convention. It seems to me that the lack of any definition might give rise to ambiguity in connection with the distributors of motion pictures and the producers of straight plays. As hon. members are aware, a book or a piece of music may be the subject of copyright, and then if either is worked into a film those interested may copyright their film. Can the minister make it clear that this term will not apply to distributors of motion picture films?

We are using in our statute the very words which are used in the con-22110-155J
vention. "Dramatico-musical" is a term of the convention; "musical" is also a term of the convention. In our statute we have defined "dramatic" and "musical," and I think it is very clear from those definitions that when a work is both dramatic and musical it is "dramatico-musical." That is the best explanation I can furnish my hon. friend. It will have to be left to the courts to construe. Perhaps those learned gentlemen to whom my hon. friend has referred as occasionally sitting at Berne and passing judgment on all the rest of the earth, might be invited to give their opinion on this term.

Subsection 2 of section
10 reads:
Whenever in the opinion of the minister, after an investigation and report by a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act

And so on. I take it that that is a commissioner appointed by the minister?

No. The minister can only appoint a commissioner to inquire into his own department. The first part of the Inquiries Act has to do with a public inquiry under a commissioner appointed by the governor in council. The investigation contemplated by this subsection must certainly be ordered by the governor in council.
How is the machinery started? Is there an investigation and report by the commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act?
Yes.
I take it that that report is made by the commissioner after somebody had complained that the act was being violated?
Certainly.

In my opinion this subsection does not make it clear how you get your machinery in motion. The opening words of the subsection are:
Whenever in the opinion of the minister, after an investigation and a report by a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act,-
The minister starts in after the commissioner has reported?

His opinion is expressed
after the commissioner has reported, but there is interim jurisdiction in the governor in council under part I of the Inquiries Act to institute an inquiry into any matter of public interest.
Copyright Act

Do I understand the minister to mean that apart from any jurisdiction conferred either upon the governor in council or upon the minister by this subsection, an inquiry might be started under the present Inquiries Act?
Quite so.

Then what is contemplated by this section is an inquiry started under the present Inquiries Act, and the report of the commissioner 'being brought to the attention of the minister. After considering the report he may be of opinion that certain restrictions should be placed upon the offending company. I am calling the minister's attention to the fact that the section here does not in my opinion, after a careful reading of it, make the necessary provision. If he is satisfied that under the Inquiries Act, there is jurisdiction now,-
I am so advised.
If he is not relying on this section alone, I am satisfied.

I am not relying on this
for authority to have the commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act, as such authority to have inquiries held under the act already exists in our statute law. If an investigation is held-and anyone can ask to have an inquiry under the Inquiries Act- and the report thereon of the commissioner, in the opinion of the minister, justifies further action, then the minister must recommend to the governor in council to have such action taken. Every safeguard is, I think, taken to see that everything proper shall be done in dealing with the matter.

speechtext: Shall section 10 carry?

Section 10 does not
carry except on division.

On division.
Section agreed to on division.
On section 11-Copies for library.
Mr. CAHA'N:	This is simply a provision
that two books shall be deposited with the library.

The minister refers to the provision in section 11 for copyrighting which, as is evident, requires that the publisher of every book, within three months after its publication, shall deliver or cause to be delivered at his own expense to
	*
the librarian of parliament certain copies of his work. Obviously there is something that is printed which is being delivered. Similarly, if it is desired to procure copyright of photographs or musical compositions, something again is printed.
This has nothing to do with the granting of copyright.

I took it that
was the meaning. Perhaps the minister will indicate whether or not there is to be in the act as completed any provision empowering the issue of copyright in dramatic works by the deposit of typewritten copies of the work, similar to the provision which is in force in Washington, and has been in force there, to my knowledge, for at least twenty years.

I have made no change
whatever with regard to the procuring of copyright in Canada. I may be simply displaying my, own ignorance, but I was under the impression that one could secure copyright in Canada by presenting a typewritten copy of any work and registering it as such.

I regret to say
that I have seen cases of that kind fail.

If so, the matter can be
dealt with under the regulations which the governor in council may be prepared to make. And certainly that should be done. I know that newspaper companies, publishing companies, present for copyright simply the ordinary first impression of the type. I should think that would apply. If not, I will see whether we cannot deal with the situation definitely by order in council, because it should be dealt with.

I do not suppose the
Secretary of State would for one moment entertain the idea that failure on the part of the publisher to comply with this section would in the least impair his right in the copyright.
No, no.

It is merely a pious wish. I may say for the benefit of my hon. friend from Ottawa that I am glad to see, although it is stipulated in this section that two copies shall be deposited, that no redress or penalty has been provided in the case of failure on the part of the publisher to deposit two books. This is one case where we can agree that it is a good thing no redress is provided for. As I say, it is merely a pious wish.

Section agreed to.

Copyright Act
On section 12-Adherence to Rome copyright convention.

I have a few remarks to make in connection with this section. In view of the opinions I have expressed in this matter I should perhaps refer for a moment to the judgment of the Privy Council in the case of the Canadian Performing Right Society versus Famous Players. According to our system of constitutional law, an international convention cannot alter nor supersede our own national law; and to be effective it must be incorporated in our own law. We have adhered to the Rome convention, and we are about to ratify this one. I may express now in the words of my hon. friend, a pious hope that, when this ratification is given, under the guidance of the present minister the operation of the law will be valid from the start. The last time there were a number of omissions and I trust that on this occasion the same thing will not recur. Now, we can legislate in any way we desire with respect to our own nationals. We make an exception in regard to unionist authors, and when we do so we must not legislate in their respect in any manner that might be in contravention of the Berne convention. If we do legislate with respect to them, then we must be careful to follow out the proper directions; and in order that there may be no mistake about it we must exclude them from the operation of that law. In other words we must clearly indicate in our Copyright Act those sections which affect nationals only, and clearly state that any such enactments will not affect unionist authors or their rights.
What is that quotation?

It will please my hon. friend when I tell him that the direction for so proceeding is given by the international bureau of Berne in its official organ, Le Droit d'Auteur of May 15, 1929, at page 57 in the comments on the judgment of the Privy Council in re the Canadian Performing Right Society versus Famous Players.
In conclusion I wish to make this statement. The convention has set out in a number of articles those things which under the International convention we are bound to do. These directions are imperative, and it is incumbent upon us, if we desire to remain in the convention, to follow them. This bill, No. 4, fails to follow these prescriptions in the instances I shall indicate. This may be a little tiresome but I wish to get it on the record, because it represents a complete expression of my views.
First, subsection 3 of article II of the Rome convention directs that:
The countries in the union shall be bound to make provision for the protection of the above mentioned works.
The Canadian Copyright Act as it stands now and, also, bill No. 4, fail to comply with these stipulations. I have gone through the articles of the convention, and in order to save time I have put these views in writing, indicating every one of the directions whereby, according to the Berne convention, we shall be bound. And I will show that we are following none of them.
Is the hon. member dealing with the bill or the Copyright Act as a whole?

I am discussing section 12 of the bill which has reference to our adherence to the Berne convention. I say that under the terms of the law as it stands at present, and under this bill as we now have it, we have not complied with the directions of the convention.
The hon. member is reviewing the whole scope of the Copyright Act as it stands on the statute.
Yes.
That seems almost irrelevant.

No. I submit that the law is in such a state that we cannot adhere to the convention.
Secondly, article III directs that "the countries in the union shall be bound to make provisions for the protection of photographic works and of works produced by a process analogous to photography." The present act, as well as bill 4, fail to comply with this direction.
I think they comply with it.

Very well; I say they do not. Thirdly, article VI bis of the Rome convention directs that the means of redress for safeguarding these rights-that is, the moral rights-shall be regulated by the country where protection is claimed. We have not included in the present legislation the means of redress stipulated by the Rome convention.
I submit that we have.

Fourth. Article 9 of the Rome convention directs that the legal consequences of the breach of these obligations, that is, the obligations respecting the press articles and other works published in the newspapers or periodicals, shall be determined by the laws of the country where protection
Copyright Act

is claimed. This answers the question asked a moment ago by the hon. member. Bill No 4 not only fails to comply with this article 9 of the Rome convention, but fails to enact that such works published in newspapers or periodicals shall be protected.
Does my hon. friend contend that newspaper articles copyrighted in Canada are not protected?

They are not protected in the manner provided by the Rome convention.
Fifth. Subsection 2 of article 2 of the Rome convention reads:
Translations, adaptations, arrangements of music and other reproductions in an altered form of a literary or artistic work, as well as collections of different works, shall be protected as original works without prejudice to the rights of the author of the original work.
There is no provision in this bill or in the Copyright Act for the protection of these works.
Sixth. This bill introduces into our act as principle in complete violation of the Rome convention and in complete violation of the fundamental principle of copyright, by giving many in clause 6 the right to use works without the consent of the author or of his assignee.
Seventh. This bill contains in clause 10 another principle in violation of the Rome convention, namely, the imposition upon the authors' collecting agency of so many formalities as to preclude them from functioning.
Eighth. This bill fails to remove from the present act the words "for private profit" which appear in subsection 3 of section 17, and in subsection 2 of section 26, which words prevent infringed authors from securing the redress prescribed by the Rome convention.
Ninth. The present bill fails to provide, in clause 12 thereof, the means for properly and effectively applying to Canada the provision contained in the Rome convention.
In order to facilitate the passing of the bill in time to allow our ratification of the Rome convention, I will support it with the reservations to which I have referred. However, I am confident that it will not be long before steps are taken by the proper authorities to bring these objections before a competent tribunal to test the soundness of the bill which we are about to pass.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to go over any of the ground which has been covered so thoroughly by the hon. members of the committee who have devoted

almost three weeks of their time to a discussion of this bill. The subject matter of the bill is highly controversial. Nearly twenty years ago I had something to do with the preparation and submission of a copyright bill and I realize the difficulties which the committee, and especially the Chairman, have had to contend with. It happens not infrequently that expediency cuts across logic-and equity. I do not say that the authors have received unfair treatment, but this bill certainly does not give them that which they have a right to expect if we are to adhere to the provisions of the Rome convention. I shall not go further than to say that I should like to file a caveat and make it clear that while this bill may be the best that can be obtained at the present time, it is not considered by the authors to be satisfactory or entirely equitable.
Mr. 'GAGNON:	Mr. Chairman, I concur
fully in the remarks of the hon. member for Stanstead. It is quite true that this bill is a decided step forward, but at the same time, as the hon. the Secretary of State has said, it is a compromise, and I regret to say that at times such compromises are made at the expense of the authors. I congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) upon the very able study he has made of this matter. Any lawyer who has practised ten or fifteen years knows that there is no country where the rights of authors are less protected than in Canada. I know that you, sir, have with success defended theatre owners as against authors; I have had such an experience and in most of the cases the rights of the authors have not been considered. The hon. member for Ottawa has cited a large number of authorities to show that in the United States, in France and in England infringers receive sentences of up to three years' imprisonment-in France the benefits of the offender [DOT]are confiscated for the benefit of the author -while in Canada an infringer may be faced with a mere fine of only ten dollars. I hope the Secretary of State can assure the committee that within a short time the necessary legislation will be passed to give proper means of redress to the authors. I heard the very eloquent speech delivered yesterday by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell), and I could not but think it is a shame that an author such as the hon. member, who has had his works published in all parts of the world, cannot be properly protected in this country. Mr. Chairman, I am not an author; my attainments are very humble, I

The Budget-Mr. Brasset
have never indulged in literature other than political speeches-I do not think they are fit material for copyright-but I am speaking because I think that some hon. members on this side of the house should express the opinion that the rights of the authors should be protected to a greater extent.
Section agreed to.

One cannot promise that a general revision of the Copyright Act will be undertaken, but certainly I would not like to undertake it myself after the experience of the last three or four months. It would require a great deal of time and study.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, June 5, consideration of the motion of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ralston.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with much
interest, these last days, to the speeches delivered in the House by members, but I especially paid attention to the budget delivered on June 1, by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who is equally the Minister of Finance. This financial statement was impatiently and anxiously expected by the Canadian people who anticipated the fulfilment of the Conservative party's pledges and the realization of a policy of progress. I should like to make a few comments as to the effects of the budget on the people of this country and the constituency which I am privileged to represent.
Being a new member, it is the first time that I listened to a Minister of Finance delivering the budget, however, for a number of years past, long before being a member of this house, I had acquired the habit of reading in Hansard or the newspapers the Minister of Finance's budget speech.
I was therefore somewhat amazed when I heard the Prime Minister state in the house that it was the first budget speech delivered here within the last seven or eight years. I wondered why the Prime Minister made such a statement. What difference could there be between this budget and those of preceding
years, to warrant such a statement? The only conclusion I could arrive at was that in the last preceding years the Minister of Finance announced surpluses, tax reductions, prosperous fiscal years, etc., so that it must have afforded him great pleasure and satisfaction in presenting his budget. The task was not as difficult as the one which our Minister of Finance, the right hon. Prime Minister, must have experienced this year in acknowledging to the house that now that our friends, the Tories were in office, the era of surpluses was at an end and that henceforth it would be replaced by an era of deficits and taxation.
History repeats itself and it does so with a regularity which should this time, I think, open the eyes of the public.
When, in 1896, Sir Wilfrid Laurier took office, the people were overburdened with all kinds of taxes. For years past, there had been invariably and steadily deficits,-in this respect the Conservatives are very regular- the wolf was at our door. However, by degrees, thanks to the sound administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the country emerged from its state of languor, surpluses began to appear, taxation dwindled from year to year.
In 1911, prosperity was general throughout the land. But as we seem to always want a change, the people got tired of being prosperous, they wanted a change, the Conservative party assumed office and kept in power until 1921, once more the country was plunged into debt and felt the pangs of poverty. In 1921 the Liberal party was returned to power. What happened then? By degrees, notwithstanding the financial depression of the first few years, the King government applied themselves to the task of bringing back prosperity. They succeeded, and in 1924, surpluses began to appear in our finances and continued doing so during the Whole term of the Liberal regime, without ever missing a year or showing signs of any weakness.
I listened a few days ago to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) comment on the high cost of living under the Liberal administration. It is a fact, that the cost of living was higher in those days than it is to-day, but there was then work for everybody; people were working and therefore had money to spend. To-day, the cost of living is perhaps lower, but this is entirely due to the fact that the purchasing power has left us, people are without work or are forced to work for hunger wages.
As just stated, since 1923 or 1924, we had steady surpluses up to this year. At the last
The Budget-Mr. Brasset

regular session, observing t'hat depression was spreading over us, the Prime Minister of the day, the right hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, with his usual sagacity and foresight, endeavoured to give the country a budget which, in my opinion, would have saved the situation and prevented the people from falling into the greatly depressed state in which they find themselves to-day. But before this budget could be given a trial an election took place and the Conservative party was placed in office by means of pledges often referred to and which it is useless to recall, since they are always present in the memory of the great majority of the people who suffer. In taking office, the Prime Minister seemed to be in a great rush to destroy the arduous and painstaking work of the Liberal party. By an emergency session, orders in council and all possible means, he wished to wipe out all traces of the good work done by his predecessors, he endeavoured to destroy the monument erected to prosperity by the Liberal party, in order t'hat he might impress the country with his personal policy. And the result is, that the first Conservative budget presents the country with a deficit of $75,000,000.
Is this the reason why the Conservatives were put in office? We had yearly surpluses and the Tory government plunges the country into debt. Was this the mission entrusted to them on July 28, last?
Furthermore, from 1924, the Liberals had decreased taxation from year to year. Thanks to the great perseverance of a statesman like the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who wished the welfare of this country, the sales tax which was then six per oent was reduced as low as one per cent. The postal stamps which Laurier had already reduced from three to two cents and which later had again been raised to three cents by the Conservative party, were once more reduced to two cents by the Liberal party. Excise stamps on cheques were reduced considerably as everybody knows. The income tax was gradually lowered from year to year and so far as imported articles, such as farm implements, gasoline motors, etc., the customs duty was largely reduced in order to help the farmers and fishermen.
The Conservative party after assuming office, at their very first session, not only raised the postal tax stamp to three cents; increased the sales tax from one per cent to four per cent; reintroduced former taxes, those advocated by their friends and abolished by the Liberals; but they bring forth new taxes, which had never been levied before by any 
party. Was this what the Conservative party promised in July last? Was this why they were elected?
I heard some one the other day, mention the duty on tea. The King government had abolished the duty on tea imported from a British possession. We are all aware that tea is a popular drink to those who cannot afford a more expensive beverage.
The Prime Minister puts a duty of four cents when this article is imported from a British country and eight cents when imported from a foreign country. So that, heretofore, with the duty and the sales tax combined the consumer will have to pay eight or twelve cents to the government for each pound of tea purchased.
The Prime Minister again, at the emergency session in the autumn, promised that the taxes levied would not affect the prices of commodities. As a measure to protect Canadian industry, this caps the climax, since everybody knows that this country does not grow tea, has never grown any and will never grow it!
This is not all, sir, the country has a deficit, the Bennett government has plunged the country into debts, and we must resort to taxes to find money. Who is to bear the burden, on whom will these taxes fall? Will it be on the wealthy class, those who can better bear the burden of taxation? No, sir. As it might be expected from a Conservative government and the past policy advocated by its leaders, it will be the poorer classes which will be called upon to bear the greater portions of these taxes. Indeed, the wealthy class, the millionaires, those who have incomes of many hundreds of thousands of dollars per year, those who live in luxury and do not know what to do with their money, these people, I state, find that their burden is becoming lighter, their taxes are reduced, while the poor people find theirs increasing out of all proportions.
Let us for instance, take the great majority of the people of this country-or to be more specific let us take the rural districts in Quebec, which are mostly composed of farmers and fishermen-there are not five per cent of these people who will ever be called upon to pay the income tax. On the other hand, each time that the head of a family wishes to purchase a bag of flour to feed his children, each time he buys a pair of boots, each time he purchases anything he must pay a tax to the government. For every dollar spent by the poor farmer or fisherman the government will receive four, five, six or ten cents more than they received last year. Was

The Budget-Mr. Brasset
this what the Conservatives promised last July? Was this why they were elected? It is not simply through necessity, because of the exigencies of the hour, that the Prime Minister has struck at the poor ratepayer by levying new taxes. It is also because he is thus inclined or if you prefer on principle, as his own words spoken during the session 1926-27 will prove, just before being chosen leader of the Conservative party. The following is what he says at page 401 of Hansard, February 27, 1927:
My idea is this. It is not original at all. You may have seen it presented by the late Sir Edmund Walker in addresses lie made to the shareholders of his bank from time to time.
I think, it is the Bank of Commerce.
He believed in a universal turn-over tax, a tax by which every man who buys something will be able to make some contribution, a percentage levy. It is simple, it is universal, it is convenient, it is equal, it is easily collected -it has all the qualifications that were mentioned by the late Adam Smith-
(Equality, universal, convenient and economic.)

and in addition to that it meets with modern conditions, and will help solve many of the diificulties that we have in this country to-day.
Mr. Bennett continues:	.
Until men and women have a realization of the money that the state is spending, and where the money comes from, there will not be that appreciation of the difficulties and responsibilities of government that is so essential for the maintenance of this dominion, and I do suggest that the Minister of Finance would be well advised to consider whether or not-there is still time-he could not devise some tax along those lines that would not have the objectionable features that attach to the so-called nuisance tax or to the sales tax as such. As between the sales tax and a tax upon turnover, which includes a tax upon everything that men buy, you would be able to get revenue more readily by a turn-over tax, and in larger quantities, and you would be able to make a clearance in the income tax.
Mr. Bennett, the present Prime Minister added these words as a closing remark:
I do say that it is wholly an erroneous proposition to say to the people of this country that the poor man should pay no taxes, and then say that he should vote. No man should vote who does not pay tax, and every man who votes should pay taxes, and, as a corollary every man who pays taxes should vote.
In 1921. Mr. Bennett desired no sales tax yet, in 1931, not only he levies a sales tax but increases it. However, what he has always forcibly advocated is taxing the poor. That is why he strongly urges the passing of these measures, this year.
The government endeavoured to palliate, to a certain extent, the disastrous effect of its deficit, by granting some slight compensation
to the west and the maritime provinces. It favours the latter by increasing the duty on coal imports and it promises a rebate on the freight rates of wheat exports. But what benefit does Quebec get from these grants? Her only benefit will be to pay more for fuel without any compensation whatsoever; and it wheat sells a little higher, owing to this government measure, the ratepayers of Quebec and Ontario will have to pay dearer for their flour. I am in favour of any advantage which the west or the maritime provinces may derive from the government's action, but I should certainly like to see my native province have its share. The other provinces should not be the only ones to benefit by the Conservative government's legislation, Quebec should also be included. In this case no favour is shown to Quebec. Nothing, unless it is increase in taxation.
The government intends to complete the construction of certain highways in Ontario and in the west. Quebec built her own highways at considerable cost, so that if the Conservative government builds highways in Ontario and the west, the province of Quebec will be forced to pay its quota in taxes for roads in other parts of the country without any benefit to herself. Nothing for Quebec, unless it is increased taxation. Thus does the Prime Minister fulfil his pledges, no doubt to thank Quebec for having sent 25 members to support him. In 1926, the Conservatives carried only four or five counties, while last year Quebec was generous enough to present Mr. Bennett with 25 seats, thus assuring him a working majority-and he thanks Quebec by [DOT] granting her nothing. The people of Quebec have been deceived, they will remember, the country will also remember.
The most important problem of this country at present, is unemployment. I read the budget speech through and not a single word is to be found dealing with that problem; the Prime Minister had talked so much about unemployment in the last election that he probably was sick of hearing it mentioned- perhaps he felt somewhat shy on the subject. That is why he brushed aside unemployment and the unemployed.
Last year he made them a gift of $20,000,000; he thinks it is enough. Although this policy produced practically no results for the country, although the number of unemployed has not decreased-on the contrary-although work is getting scarcer every day, nothing is said, nothing is done; parliament has now been in session almost three months and notwithstanding all the appeals of distress which reach us from the four corners of the
The Budget-Mr. Brasset

country, nothing indicates that the Prime Minister or the government have any knowledge of conditions which now prevail.
Before closing my remarks, sir, I deem it my duty to strongly protest on behalf of my constituency and those who are in need and who had hoped that the government would fulfil the pledges made last year.
As I stated in some of my speeches during the election, and again stated in the house, in a speech which I delivered at the outset of the session, smiles of contentment seem to creep over the faces of members of the government, for instance, at present, over the face of the Hon. Arthur Sauve, at the very mention of unemployment. If anyone who champions the cause of the people, of those who are in distress, could but see for instance the smile which I perceive, at this moment on the lips of the Postmaster General, he would rebuke the minister, under the present circumstances for laughing at the distress of the people.
I deem it, sir, my duty to once more protest and I do so not only 'because the government is not stirring itself to help the people, but also because members of the government smile when we mention the distress of the people. That the government are helpless, so much the worse for them; but if the government care not for the people, there will come a day of reckoning. The present government have not fulfilled their pledges, they have not alleviated the prevailing distress; they have increased taxation and customs and excise duties; they have therefore won the people's votes by false pretences, and before long the ' people will rise and act accordingly.
Mr. J. R. MacNICOfL (Toronto Northwest) : In the tariff proposals brought down by the Minister of Finance on the first of June, the government has gone a long way towaj-ds the goal of adequate tariff protection. Those proposals, coupled with the government's determination to safeguard the public ' against price exploitation, I am sure have met with approval throughout the country. Last fall, after the government took office, they called a special session and arranged for the Imperial conference and, in my humble opinion, their achievements in their few months of office have met with public approval.
As one who has served in industry for many years, I think I have some conception of the opinion of those who work in industry, and I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in few places will the proposals of the government, as brought down in the budget, be more carefully read and studied than in the factories and

offices of Canada. I am satisfied that in those places the budget will be called a workman's and business man's budget, and in the term business man I include of course, agriculturists.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have called this a millionaire's budget, but the effects we can already observe from the tariff readjustment-made last fall in the way of increasing employment and stimulating industry indicate that we can confidently look for a still greater increase in employment and still greater activity in industry as a result of the present budget proposals.
Having had a background of many years' experience in industry I think I am qualified to state the viewpoint of the workers in factory and office. What is the viewpoint of the workers? If I may I should like to allude to the old plant in which it was my pleasure and experience to serve for many years. I wonder what a worker looking out of the windows of the old Dominion Radiator and Boiler Company plant would see. Probably hon. members would be interested in his view. He would see the smokestacks of many other industries in which, if he so desired, he might be employed and in which his fellow workmen are engaged. Offhand I can call to my mind the names of such large industries as the Canadian General Electric Company; Gray Forgings and Stampings Limited, manufacturers of tools; the Standard Sanitary Manufacturing Company; C. A. Dunham Company Limited; The Gold Medal Furniture Manufacturing Company; the Easy Washing Machine Company; The A.B. Ormsby Company, Limited; The Hamilton Gear and Machine Company; and the John T. Hepburn Company Limited. Then, about a quarter of a mile away he would see the plant of the McGregor-Mclntyre Iron Works Limited, and the Paton and Baldwin Textile Company. Those plants, Mr. Speaker, employ a great many men. If a worker were to observe the routine of the receiving office of the manufacturing concern in which he is employed he would see entering his plant either iron, brass, wire, cotton, woollen goods, lumber or other raw products which enter into the commodities to which the worker applies his labour and intelligence. In passing, Mr. Speaker, may I make the statement that there are no more intelligent workers in the world than those men and women employed in Canadian industry. There are none who give more serious consideration to the task they have in hand. Having worked with them for more than twenty-five years I have a very high regard for -their industry and integrity. If the workman employed in industry were to

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
visit the shipping office he would see gomg out to many communities the finished product to which he had added his intelligence and labour. The Canadian worker is not an agitator. He is neither a book economist nor a book theorist. He is practical, however; he knows that work is life's currency. He knows that anything which interferes either with the receipt of the raw product upon which he works in his plant or with the application of his skill and intelligence to the goods. themselves or to their shipment takes from him the opportunity to work and to earn wages.
Let me refer to the 14,000 workers employed in the manufacture of rubber goods. This particular industry enjoys a tariff protection of 22i per cent, 30 per cent and 35 per cent, depending upon the tariff class under which the goods fall. Through the operation of a tariff those 14,000 employees are enabled to work in their plants and are in a position to manufacture nearly 100 per cent of the automobile tires and other rubber goods required in Canada. For home consumption goods are manufactured to the value of $45,000,000 and for export, to the value of about $21,000,000, for distribution in the different markets of the world. This industry is able to compete in the markets of the world and at the same time charges only a reasonable price in the home market. Before leaving my remarks on this industry may I say that the rubber workers are almost 100 per cent for tariff protection. They know if it were not for the protection they receive through tariff duties the rubber industry of Canada would be crucified.
I wish now to direct the attention of hon. members to an industry which was only recently revived in Carleton Place, Ontario. I refer to the old plant of the Hawthorn Mills, Limited, which manufactured woollen products. That old plant was put out of commission in 1922 as a result of tariff reductions in that year on cottons and woollens. In the same year twenty-five other plants manufacturing about 45 per cent of the total woollen manufactures of Canada were also forced out. Recently the Hawthorn plant was reopened by an English firm. Although I am not sure of the name, I think they are known as the Hirst Company. Some of the old employees, who about nine years ago were put out of employment through the reduction in tariffs, have been taken on again. Imagine any man trying to convince those employees that a tariff is not good for them. Imagine any man trying to convince those men who
have received work after nine years of more or less idleness caused by free trade that the tariff measures are not in the best interests of Canadians.
I rose, however, more particularly to direct my remarks to conditions in the iron and steel industry, because it was with that industry I was connected for a period of about twenty-five years. I am familiar with the industry from the bottom to the top, from the moulding shop to the high executive offices. For tariff purposes the iron and steel industry is divided into about 100 different items. In connection with the seven principal items of which we import into Canada foreign goods made by foreigners in foreign plants the totals amount to many millions. Those goods are imported to the detriment of Canadian labour to an extent to which I shall now direct the attention of hon. members. The figures I am now about to quote are approximate figures for the last fiscal year of the late government ending March 31, 1930:
Vehicles, composed principally
of iron and steel	 $74,000,000
Machinery (apart from agricultural machinery)	 65,000,000
Rolling mill products	 55,000,000
Farm machinery	 30,000,000

These various commodities represent a total import value of $250,000,000, of which about $35,000,000 worth came in absolutely free of duty.
May I digress for a moment to deal with the statement that I have heard from speakers in this house that a policy of protection would interrupt and indeed prohibit trade with other nations. Nothing of the kind. I submit that no matter what tariff Canada has she will at all times have to import approximately a billion dollars' worth of goods.
From my knowledge of Canadian workmen and Canadian executives I have no hesitation in saying that under this new tariff they can with their present plants and equipment manufacture an additional $50,000,000 worth of steel goods. Almost daily we see in the newspapers reports that steel companies in the United States are going to erect new plants in Canada or increase their present branch plants here. Perhaps the most notable of these is the United States Steel Company, which has a plant at Ojibway, near Windsor. They are now completing a large mill which they started some time ago in the hope that the government would give adequate protection to the steel and iron industry of Canada. They know that now they can go ahead and bring

Now, Mr. Speaker, what will an additional
