subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR

speechtext: Mr. MAURICE BRASSET (Gaspe) moved the second reading of Bill No. 42, to amend the Bankruptcy Act as respects locality of a debtor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
This bill relates only to
the province of Quebec and has to do with the locality of a debtor in bankruptcy. The

Bankruptcy Act
object of the bill is to oblige the creditor to present his petition in bankruptcy only in the district having jurisdiction over the locality or domicile of the debtor. In other words, a person wanting to have a debtor declared insolvent would be required, if this bill were adopted, to present his petition in the judicial district wherein the insolvent carries on his business.. As the law stands at the present time a petition can be presented anywhere in Quebec, before any court in the province in addition to a court of civil jurisdiction. For example, if the debtor resides in Gaspe, a creditor in the Province of Quebec residing in Montreal, or even in Hull, at the other extremity of the province, may present his petition in Montreal, or in Hull, as the case may be, to have the debtor declared insolvent. The debtor cannot leave his place of residence and come down to Hull to defend his petition in the court there. I might mention by way of illustration a case that occurred recently in Chicoutimi where a petition was presented by a creditor while another creditor presented another petition in Montreal. Both petitions were granted, so that in two places at the same time the debtor was declared bankrupt. The debtor failed to respond to both petitions, with the result that he was sued in Montreal a second time. He had become a bankrupt in Chicoutimi but the proceedings were carried on in Montreal. These proceedings should be carried on at the place where the debtor resides. If a civil action is taken in the courts it is conducted at -the place where the defendant resides and it is only justice to a debtor that he should be sued in the district where he resides.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: If the debtor should happen to be a corporation with its head office outside of the province of Quebec, where would the petition for bankruptcy be presented, according to this bill?

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
The application would
be made at the place where the debtor carries on his business in the province of Quebec.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
Suppose the corporation
was doing business in three or four different places in the province of Quebec, at what point would the application be made?

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
If the company has no
head office in the province of Quebec the petition would be served at the head office. The civil code provides that this service must be made at the head office; if that head office is in Toronto, it would be served in Toronto, but if the head office is in Quebec the petition would be served at that place.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to object to the second reading of the bill; this is a legal matter and as a layman I should not like to pronounce on a measure of this kind. I have before me a letter from la chambre de commerce de Montreal which states an objection to this bill on the ground that it would considerably increase the costs of procedure. This letter is in French, and I will read it in the original language. It is as follows: (Translation):
The Council of the Chamber of Commerce of Montreal strongly protest against the enactment of Bill B "amending the Bankruptcy Act as respects the locality of a debtor" which is, at present, before parliament, and request me to ask you to kindly_ support this protest so as to prevent this bill being enacted.	.	. .
At the last session of the provincial legislature, a similar bill was thrown out at our request and for the following reasons: That the choice of the locality of a debtor in bankruptcy matters, if it were admitted would entail considerable travelling and other expenses inherent to the winding up of an estate and this, at the expense of the creditors. Moreover this would increase the law costs which are already very high. In every way this amendment would be prejudicial to the aim sought by the said Bankruptcy Act: the prompt and efficient winding up of the business.
These considerations militated in favour ot the rejection of the bill by the provincial legislature and it seems to us that they should carry the same weight with you.
Our council therefore kindly ask. you to request or support the rejection of said bill B which is of a nature to hinder considerably trade.	.
In anticipation, please accept our smcerest thanks.
I do not wish to comment on this letter nor do I endorse it; I merely want to place it on Hansard for the consideration of those who are discussing this measure.
Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix-Saguenay) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I
think that the bill moved by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Brasset) is entitled to the favourable consideration of the house. As representative of an agricultural county which is at a distance from the large centres, I deem it my duty to support this bill which, in certain cases, considering the present act and the amendments thereto, it might be helpful to the people of my county. I fail to discover what difficulties it could embody, although the fees might, in certain cases, be higher. One must bear in mind that the farmers and residents of rural districts might be caught napping if the act remains as it is and thereby put to a greater expense. For these reasons the house should favourably consider this -bill and enact it without any
Bankruptcy Act

change. Moreover, it has been considered and approved by the Senate, and I am also aware that the same measure was submitted in previous years to the former administration. For certain reasons it was found impossible to introduce then this bill in the house, as it should have been in the shape of an amendment, included in the general bill, to amend the Bankruptcy Act. I think that the bill such as it is should be enacted.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now under discussion deserves the support of all hon. members of this house. As the law stands to-day it creates a real injustice towards the small merchant and small creditors living outside of the big cities in the province of Quebec. A man may be declared a bankrupt in the county of Gaspe, where the hon. member who supports this bill resides, and he can be forced to attend all the proceedings which may be carried on in the city of Montreal. That is not fair. The tribunals of the province of Quebec, including I think the supreme court, have decided that according to the law as it stands to-day a district means the province. I maintain that it is not fair to force a man residing in the counity of Gaspe to come to the city of Montreal or perhaps to the city of Hull to attend the proceedings in bankruptcy. That is an anomaly which should be corrected. I do not agree with the arguments advanced in the letter just read by the former Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret). There would be no increase in the legal costs if the proceeedings were caried on in the district where the debtor lives or has his principal place of business. The wholesale merchants find it to their advantage to go out and sell their goods in Gaspe, and it would be only fair when there is difficulty about their accounts or when a bankruptcy occurs that they should go to that place and fight the action should there be any dispute. There is more in this bill than a mere question of law or a mere question of legal principle and judicial jurisdiction. We hear complaints about the centralization of all activities in one or two places throughout Canada. In my opinion the province of Ontario owes its success to the fact that business and all other activities have been decentralized. In the province of Quebec we have been suffering from a centralization of almost everything in two or three places. Speaking more particularly for those who reside in the rural sections of the province, I submit that there should be more decentralization and a chance given to those who live in the rural sections. After all, the strength of a country or 
of a province depends upon its rural sections. We all on certain occasions during the year ask the farmers to remain on the land; we ask those who are at present in the cities to go back to the land; indeed, we preach to them that their only salvation is to do so. It is very hard in certain parts of our country to preach with any measure of success this gospel of decentralization. If we deprive all the rural centres of their activities as well as their attractiveness; if we destroy the jurisdiction of the tribunals existing in all the rural districts, I do not think we are helping our country to regain its prosperous condition, and, after all, we are not rendering any measure of assistance or support to the big centres.
I repeat: there is in the bill more than the mere question of jurisdiction. If the members on the government side will support the measure, they will be making a step forward towards helping to give the rural sections of Quebec a certain degree of importance. In the rural districts of Quebec we are deprived of tribunals; we are deprived of judges.

speechtext: Who was responsible for that?

speechtext:
That was a mistake which was made, and I never agreed with it, because a judge residing in a small locality helps to maintain the standard of living and the morals of the people living there. He is an arbiter above political parties, above all the troubles connected with municipal or social affairs in the locality. When he walks along the street the people say: Here is the judge-they look upon him with respect.
Mr. PO'ULIOT:	Provided he is a good
judge.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
Under present conditions a judge appears there occasionally, perhaps for a day or two once a month. It is said openly that for some of the judges the railway time table is their highest authority. It is time we afforded an opportunity to the rural sections of Quebec to keep within each judicial district the legal business pertaining to it. It is not fair to centralize everything in the big cities.
I know big corporations and financial organizations, the Montreal Chamber of Commerce and the Montreal Board of Trade are strongly opposed to this legislation; but all these organizations are to a certain extent local in their character; they look after their own affairs, and we cannot blame them for not having any consideration for the rural sec-

Bankruptcy Act
tions of Quebec. But I think it is time that parliament realized the situation in which the rural residents of our province are placed at the present time. This bill has been passed in the Senate at possibly three but certainly two consecutive sessions, and it is about time we adopted it.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: Under the present law is there any difference between Ontario and Quebec? Can the same thing happen in Ontario, or, if not, will the hon. member explain the difference?

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: The same thing can happen in Ontario. A man living in the city of Windsor being in a bad situation from a business point of view, may be forced to come to Ottawa to answer a petition in bankruptcy, and all the proceedings in regard to the case may be had in this city. We do not, however, want to make the scope of this measure too wide. I have been in sympathy for a long time with the principle. It was thought probably it would be best to start by making an exception in the case of the province of Quebec-that, also, as the law in Quebec is quite different from that in the other provinces, it would be more justifiable, at least as a beginning, to have the law amended for that province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: My suggestion in regard to this bill which came to the house from the upper chamber would be that the matter be allowed to stand for the present session, as within a reasonable time, probably next session, I think there will have to be a more or less general revision of the Bankruptcy Act as it appears on the statute book. We know that almost every session since the year 1920, when the act was originally passed, one or two or more amendments have been made to it. I do not favour continuously amending the Bankruptcy Act or any other law, but from the numerous communications which I have received, I realize there are many respects in which the present act might be revised and improved. Speaking in regard to this point on a former occasion this session I think I intimated to the house that in my view a committee of the house should be appointed, probably at the next session, to consider all the suggestions which have been offered in recent times concerning amendments to the general act. This bill applies only to the province of Quebec. It must be pointed out that the Bankruptcy Act is not in its first essential an act for the benefit, or relief, or convenience of the debtor. The -most interested parties in an insolvency or bankruptcy proceeding are certainly the creditors.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, there are also creditors residing in the rural districts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
I am quite well aware of that, but as a rule we find that a majority of the creditors are in the larger cities where wholesale businesses are carried on. I mention this fact only because it should be borne in mind that it is not altogether the convenience of the unfortunate debtor that we have to consider, while I admit that the act as framed and as passed by the house was an act greatly in favour of the insolvent, more so than any law we previously had in Canada, because it provides under certain conditions for the discharge of the honest insolvent. In the act as it is at present framed in regard to this particular section, there may be defects and there may be room for improvement, but the present act is pretty broad. It reads as follows in regard to the locality of the debtor:
"Locality of a debtor," whether a bankrupt or assignor, means (1) the principal place where the debtor has carried on business during the year immediately preceding the date of the presentation against him of a bankruptcy petition or the making by him of an authorized assignment.
That is the district in his own locality where he has carried on business for a year.
(2)	The place where the debtor has resided during the year immediately preceding the date of the presentation against him of a bankruptcy petition or the making by him of an authorized assignment.
If he does not live in the exact place where he carries on business, then the locality is the place of his domicile.
(3) In cases not coming within (1) or (2), the place where the greater portion of the property of such debtor is situate.
That, I think, is a fairly comprehensive arrangement which is prescribed under the present law. There is much to be said in favour of what the hon. member for Richelieu, who has just taken his seat, has remarked in regard to convenience in certain judicial districts or inconvenience, through the lack of constitution of sufficient judicial districts in certain provinces of Canada. But no one knows better than my hon. friend that the objection which my hon. friend has outlined to the house in this respect is one that lies entirely within the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec. This house cannot interfere in any way with the judicial arrangements in Quebec or in any other province
Bankruptcy Act

in Canada. The administration of the law, both civil and criminal, is entirely within the hands of the provincial authorities. The constitution of provincial courts, the number of judges, the districts over which the judges shall preside, and all interior arrangements for administration of the law are within the hands of the Quebec government. The premier of the province of Quebec, who is also the attorney general of that province, can remedy any difficulty in these interior arrangements at any moment he sees fit. The only power of this parliament in regard to judges is to -appoint and to pay them. If any grievance exists in the respect complained of in the province of Quebec, this parliament cannot remedy it. We cannot decree that the judges shall live or reside or hold court in this or that district, or in this or that county. The province of Quebec alone can control such a situation, and if any inconvenience is caused in this regard, if it be brought to the attention of the government of the province of Quebec, I have no doubt that it will be remedied.
I may say that I likewise have received some letters objecting to the passage of this measure. I have received a letter in English similar to the letter which has been read from the chamber of commerce of Montreal, as well as letters from boards of trade in the province of Quebec, and I have replied to those letters that the matter was not likely to be dealt with at this session, but that in the near future there would probably be a general revision of the Bankruptcy Act when full consideration would be given to these proposals. What I would ask my hon. friend who is sponsoring this bill to do is to allow this bill to stand and to bring forward this proposal when there is a general revision of the Bankruptcy Act. Personally I think it not well to pass an amendment applicable to a single province as proposed by this bill. Any amendment passed should have general effect throughout Canada. I realize, of course, that this cannot be achieved in every instance, that some amendments cannot be applicable to all parts of Canada and that some exceptions will have to be m-ade, but in regard to the present bill I think it would be unwise to introduce a new provision applicable to a single province, while disregarding the practices established in other provinces. For these reasons I would ask the sponsor of this bill to allow this bill to stand until a general measure for the revision of the Bankruptcy Act can be brought forward and a committee of this house be ap-

pointed which can give consideration to this and other proposals.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): I think there has been a -great deal of misunderstanding concerning the Bankruptcy Act. Certainly if the abuses referred to- because no other term would characterize what has been described by the hon. gentleman- prevail in -Canada there might be better reasons for the bill than actually exist. A debtor may not be hailed from Gaspe to Montreal, there to bear witness to the winding up of his business. A bankruptcy petition, as pointed out by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), must be presented according to subsection 5 of section 4 of the act to the court having jurisdiction in the locality of the debtor.
Mr. -CARDIN: It has been decided by the courts that the locality means the province. The supreme court has recently decided that.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
Paragraph (y) of section 2 of the act defines " the locality of a debtor" as:
(i)	the principal place where the debtor has carried on business during the year immediately preceding ....
(ii)	the place where the debtor has resided during the year immediately preceding . . . .
(iii)	in cases not coming within (i) or (ii), the place where the greater portion of the property of such debtor is situate;
What has been attempted by this act is to determine that the " locality of a debtor " shall be the judicial district as defined by the statutes of the province of Quebec in which the debtor lives. I find that section 160 of the Bankruptcy Act gives to the governor in council the right to divide the province into bankruptcy divisions. The province of Quebec has been divided into twelve bankruptcy divisions. I have forgotten the exact number of judicial districts in the province; I think there are twenty of them. By order in council published in the official gazette, on August 25, 1923, the province of Quebec was divided into twelve bankruptcy divisions. They are: Montreal, Quebec, Beauharnois, Sherbrooke, Three Rivers, Hull, Chicouti-mi, Joliette, Roberval, Fraserville, New Carlisle and Amos. So it will be seen that these divisions are pretty evenly distributed throughout the province and a man cannot be taken outside of his own division. If the amendment passes, it will become necessary to erect a bankruptcy court in each judicial district, and it will be necessary to man from eight to fifteen more bankruptcy courts in the province

Bankruptcy Act
of Quebec, which will entail much additional expense.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: That would have to be done by the governor in council.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: It would have to be done by the governor in council. That is one reason for which I am opposed to this measure. But I think the best reason for following the suggestion of the Minister of Justice and not going further with this bill is that this is not the way to do it. If it is desired to re-subdivide the province of Quebec into twenty or twenty-five bankruptcy divisions instead of twelve, it is not necessary to have recourse to parliament. Section 160 of the act confers on the governor in council the prerogative and the right to do what it is sought to do by this legislation.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: I will read section 160, in the hope that my hon. friend will agree with me.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext: The courts have already decided against your view.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF PETITION IN LOCALITY OF DEBTOR
speechtext:
Section 160 provides:
Each province of Canada shall constitute for the purposes of this act, one bankruptcy district, but the governor in council may divide any such bankruptcy district into two or more bankruptcy divisions, and name or number them.
The governor in council has power to do that by order in council. By order in council of August 25, 1923, the province of Quebec was divided into twelve bankruptcy divisions. Now if the governor in council had the power to divide the province into twelve bankruptcy divisions, he certainly has the power to divide it into twenty or twenty-five divisions. All that is necessary to achieve the purpose of the sponsor of this bill, if one concedes that the purpose is a laudable one, is to pass an order in council repealing the order in council which divides the province into twelve bankruptcy divisions, and pass another re-subdividing it into fifteen or twenty or thirty, as the wisdom of the governor in council may dictate. I therefore suggest that the bill itself is unnecessary to achieve the purpose in view, and I doubt very much whether the purpose be a wise or a useful one, because bankruptcy, fortunately, is to a very large extent restricted to the larger industrial centres. I know there are farmers who do go into bankruptcy, but their creditors are generally near home. For these reasons I am very happy to reiterate the suggestion offered

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I entirely concur in the statement just made by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). In my opinion, if the amendment moved by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Brasset) were enacted, it would be the cause of great inconveniences and particularly to Quebec. In fact, we have in the province of Quebec a judicial system which differs from that of other provinces. It happens in certain judiciary districts of Quebec that the judges sit only at intervals of two and three months. Let us suppose that in the county of Gaspe, at New Carlisle or Gaspe, for instance, there is a petition filed under the Bankruptcy Act against a merchant; if the party concerned refused to comply or acknowledge his state of insolvency a judge would have to come to the district. Consequently, in certain districts of our province it might happen that a merchant who is bankrupt, in order to gain time, might find means of delaying action and no further steps could be taken for two, three and perhaps four months. To meet the wishes of creditors the procedure of the judicial administration in Quebec would have to be completely changed. A further inconvenience, sir, is that in wishing to protect, as it seems, the small merchant, the latter would be debarred of all protection. I listened a few moments ago to the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin)-like all his colleagues of the Liberal party, especially when it is a question of public interest-appealing once more to prejudice, rebuking us and endeavouring to have our people believe that it is a matter of struggle against large corporations or trusts. There is, at present, no question of protecting large corporations or trusts but it is one of protecting the interests of the people of Quebec. I think that the small merchant will have less protection if wholesale dealers are compelled to undertake the prosecution of bankruptcy cases in certain judicial districts where small dealers reside, because the latter will certainly hurt their credit with wholesale houses. I therefore concur, sir, in the comments which the hon. member for Stanstead made; and as the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) stated, if the government intends to amend the Bankruptcy Act, it would be wiser, I believe, to put off this measure until next session. However, should the hon. member for Gaspe persist in bringing his amendment to an issue, I shall deem it my duty to oppose it on the two following grounds: First, in the interests of the small

Bankruptcy Act

rural dealers themselves, and secondly, because of our particular judicial system in Quebec.
Mr. CHARLES E. FERLAND (Joliette) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I deem it my
duty to give my entire support to the bill which the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Brasset) has introduced. We listened a few moments ago to the objections which the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) has against the bill. I am rather amazed at his stand because I would have thought that the hon. member for Stanstead, who, it is true, practises law in Montreal, but who is nevertheless elected by a rural constituency, would first have proved himself the champion of the interests of the people of his rural section, the county of Stanstead, in preference to boosting the interests of large corporations or wholesale dealers of Montreal, who have other means at their disposal to protect themselves.
As to the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. Dorion), he practises law in the city of Quebec and it is in his habits to sponsor the interests of city folks instead of the ratepayers of rural districts.
The hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) and those on this side of the house who expressed their views on the merits of the bill under consideration, proved to us clearly that the present act should be amended, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, because it is so unfair that it practically takes away the control of all bankruptcy matters from rural creditors and debtors. The debtor and creditors of rural districts have not the means to make numerous trips to the city to protect their interests, either before the Montreal or Quebec courts, or to assignees' offices where the meetings of creditors take place. Any member of the legal profession who has had any practice in rural sections, know how numerous are the abuses committed. I could cite many examples. May I point out an instance of such abuse: a merchant residing in the village of St-Ignace-du-Lac, in the northern part of the county of Maskinonge, 75 miles distant from the town of Joliette-this person was compelled, at the request of a creditor in the city of Quebec, most likely the only creditor in that city, to travel to Quebec in order to file his schedule and make an assignment. Most of the creditors resided in Montreal, in his parish or in Joliette. The facts of the case are that the numerous creditors residing in St-Ignace-du-Lac, who had given this merchant credit were unable to make numerous

trips to Quebec to watch over their interests. The Quebec dealer had full control of this bankruptcy, he directed the proceedings and liquidated the rather large stock of this merchant, and we discovered a year or two after that the debtor had concealed about half of his stock. As to the local creditors, they practically lost everything and they have no further recourse owing to the insolvent state of the debtor. This is one instance in a thousand. The present act has been so interpreted that it allows a creditor to present its petition in bankruptcy before any court in Quebec. I see no reasons why members from other provinces should object to our passing legislation which would apply to Quebec, and more particularly to the rural sections of that province. Other provinces have no interest in preventing us from enacting certain amendments to an act which, in Quebec, has reacted unfavourably on the credit of farmers, even ruining entirely their credit.
It seems to me that members of other provinces have no interest in impeding the enactment of measures which would benefit the province of Quebee. As to members from Quebec, I frankly state that if they reside in the city of Montreal or Quebec, they cannot, if they are lawyers, oppose such a move, because they will have the advantage of pleading in bankruptcy cases in their own city, regardless of the domicile of their debtor. So far as members of rural sections, if they are in earnest in their desire to prevent the administration being centralized in large towns, their duty is to support this measure destined to help the rural district ratepayers.

Bankruptcy Act
for Stanstead that there are less bankruptcy districts than there are judicial districts in Quebec; secondly, may I mention to him that the bankruptcy districts to which he refers have never been utilized to my knowledge and that, in the general practice of the province of Quebec bar, petitions are filed in Quebec or Montreal, and the debtors are compelled to come to those cities and settle their bankruptcy affairs, with very few exceptions. What happens? Exactly what I was explaining a moment ago. The debtor- no more than the creditors of rural sections- is in no financial position to attend these creditors' meetings or to follow the litigation before the courts, so that bankruptcy affairs remain in the hands of people residing in large cities, and rural creditors can have no further redress and thereby lose all means of control.
I listened a few moments ago to the member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion) complaining of the delays which would result if the amendment was carried. Was there ever an objection so flimsy as that? We are all aware that owing to the congestion of business before the courts of Montreal and Quebec, but especially in Montreal, it is impossible to plead a case even though it be a summary one, without having to wait seven or eight months. When, in ordinary cases in Montreal, it is impossible to get a hearing within twelve to fifteen months. Such is the actual state in the large cities of the province of Quebec. In our own rural districts when a case is filed in the prothonotary's office of the superior court, it may be proceeded with within two or three months. With reference to delays, if a debtor contested a bankruptcy petition, in the Montreal district, I am sure that the creditor could not obtain judgment as quickly as he could in rural districts.
I entirely agree with the remarks made, a few moments ago, by the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin). Complaint is made, to-day, in rural sections that too much centralizing is carried on in large cities. We hear complaints as regards judicial centralization which allows judges to reside in large cities, while in rural sections we can only obtain judges for five or ten days per month. The management of the National railways centralizes all in Montreal, notwithstanding that there exists a contract which obliges the Canadian National Railway to have a superintendent and his staff at Joliette, which is a divisional point of the Canadian National Railway.
We hear complaints of the centralization of commercial and industrial corporations which is detrimental to the rural district ratepayers. What purpose is to be gained in centralizing all in Montreal and Quebec if we allow all rural districts and towns like Joliette to go to ruin.

I was
delighted to hear the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) state a few moments ago, that there would probably be a . general revision of the Bankruptcy Act, next year. I am aware that amendments have been suggested last winter by the council of the Montreal bar, but these amendments have not yet been presented to the House. I am also aware that other amendments have been considered and suggested by the Canadian Bar Association which is to meet this summer in Calgary, but even then, very few rural district lawyers will be called upon to study these amendments, and what will probably happen is that the delegates will be chosen from lawyers residing in large centres, so that it is unnecessary to await a general revision of the Bankruptcy Act to dispose of the amendment passed by the senate and at present being considered by the house.
I hope that in the general revision, it will *be suggested to leave the farmers out of the Bankruptcy Act, because I contend that pursuant to the B.NA. Act the Bankruptcy Act, so far as people not in commerce is concerned, is ultra vires and unconstitutional. In fact, in 1867, bankruptcy affairs were placed under federal control, while the province of Quebec Act with reference to the assignment of property included those in trade but not the farmers. For this reason, among others the Bankruptcy Act so far as farmers are concerned is ultra vires.

. Mr. MacNICOL: When the house rose I was just coming to the question of the value of our home market. Since the commencement of the session I have heard so much afoout the value of the overseas market that I had begun to wonder concerning the value of our. home .market. For the information of hon, members may I say that there are 700,000 employees in Canadian industry, and when we add to that number the families of those employees we account for about three and one-half million souls. On June 1, when the budget was brought down the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) gave a list of some seventy-four United States manufacturing concerns which had established branches in Canada, as a result of the increases made last fall in the tariff schedules. To that number have been added some additional American branch factories until to-day we have eighty-one American factories comprising new branches, branches which have increased in size and Canadian companies manufacturing for American concerns-all as a result of the September tariff increases. From the days when the Laurier administration assumed office, when the American manufacturers learned that the incoming Liberal administration did not intend to give freer trade, and during the time of the Borden administration, over one thousand American branch plants were established in Canada, In all there are to-day over 1,400 branches of American firms in Canada, and about seventy branches of British firms. A large number of employees are engaged1 in the manufacturing activities of those plants and that number is being added to owing to the fact that new factories are now being built.
I have here some figures in connection with several new branch plants which are being erected as a result of the tariff changes made last fall. First I shall direct the attention of hon. members to the erection of a plant at Tecumseh by a company named "Fine Foods of Canada Limited" with offices at Windsor. In the construction of that plant there have already been used 220 carloads of material principally manufactured in Canada. At the present time 150 men are engaged in the erection of the plant and it is expected that business operations will be commenced within the next month. In the coming season 200 operators will be employed in the plant; it is expected they will use during the year 175 carloads of tin cans, sugar and other materials entering into the manufacture of their product and their output will be 3,000 tons.
(Mr. Speaker.]
Estimating the length of a car to be 40 feet, those 220 cars would form a train one and three-quarter miles in length. Had only one plant been erected surely this result alone would be worth while. However there are others. Let us now consider the Canadian Ceianese Company Limited at Drummond-ville, Quebec. During the past winter a large addition was made to their plant, which became necessary through trade conditions brought about by the changes in the tariff of last fall. In the construction of that addition 375 carloads of material were used, including sand, gravel, cement, crushed stone, brick, reinforcing steel, roofing material, plumbing and heating material, and sprinkler equipment. The major portion of these materials was manufactured in other Canadian plants by Canadian workmen. If we were to estimate the length of those 375 cars we would have a train about two and three-quarter miles long. In the transportation of the materials, railroad employees and equipment would be engaged, so that not only the men engaged in the erection and operation of the plant but also those engaged in the transportation of material to the plant receive substantial benefit. In the erection of that plant 450 men were employed during the past winter.
At this time I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to some facts concerning the erection of the Campbell Soup Company Limited, factory at New Toronto. The other day after listening to one of the blue ruiu speeches in the house, and feeling that surely if we were to believe what we heard in the house there could not be any industry in Canada, I went home and drove out to view the Campbell Soup plant. May I say to my hon. friends that there is a great deal of business in Canada. This country is to-day more prosperous than any other country in the world. However had it not been for the tariff changes made last fall we would find ourselves in the unfortunate position in which other countries are now finding themselves. Now, 680 carloads of material went into that plant and 350 men were engaged in its erection. It will give employment to 180 employees.

One would think to hear some hon. members that our farmers have not anything to rely on but an export market. Let me remind them that the home market is of very great value, and is directly reflected in the buying power of the community.
I wish to spend a moment now in connection with wages in Canada as compared with those paid in competing countries. In this regard it might be of interest to quote the words of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) as reported at page 1925 of Hansard of May 9, 1924, when the hon. member spoke in the budget debate of that year. The hon. member said:
I do not favour a prohibitive tariff,-
Nor do we on this side of the house.
-but I believe in a tariff that will enable legitimate industries to live if they are efficiently conducted. I believe in that sort of a tariff also for another reason, namely, that it will give employment to our people.
And that is the reason I am in favour of a tariff, because it provides a very great deal of employment. Now what do we find in connection with wages? How are we to maintain the standard of living of the Canadian worker if he is compelled to compete

with foreign workers receiving wages at very much lower rates? In Russia, for example, the worker receives 14-4 cents per hour; in Jugoslavia he receives 16 cents; in Italy, 16 cents; in Spain, 17 cents; in Germany, 31 cents; in Holland, 35 cents; in Sweden, 43 cents and in Denmark, 45 cents. In Great Britain the worker receives 30 cents. These wages I am giving have reference to turners and fitters in the iron industry in these various countries. In Canada, for the same class of work, the worker receives 68 cents. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that there is an hon. member in this house who desires to see the standard of living in Canada reduced to the level of the average standard prevailing in these other countries. But how can we maintain a decent standard of living in this country if we do not make it possible to pay wages commensurate with such a standard? I am for good wages. The better the wages our workers receive the more competent they are likely to be and the better position will they find themselves in to buy the goods which the producers of Canada have to offer. I find that many people in Canada seem to be under the impression that the Canadian manufacturer adds the tariff to the price of his goods to determine his selling price. He does no such thing. I have an intimate knowledge of several industries in this country and I can assure the house that the prices charged are not arrived at in that manner. Take for example what the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) said in this house, as reported at page 326 of Hansard of September 17. The hon. member well said:
-I have no objection to protection; in fact I think it is necessary in this country. But when a manufacturer takes advantage of the tariff to the full extent it is time for the government, not to increase his protection, but to lower it. There are manufacturers in Canada, indeed there are several in the city of Sherbrooke, who have a protected product and who are not taking advantage of their protection to the extent of a single cent, but are selling their output to the Canadian public at exactly the same price as that at which similar goods are sold in the United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yresterday, when my hon.
friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) attempted to bring before the house the very serious condition that prevails in this country to-day, there was a good deal of opposition expressed. I note in this morning's Gazette that no less an authority than Sir George Paish uses such phrases as, "The economic

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
and financial dissolution," and the threatened "catastrophe."
It seems to me, in view of the very serious situation, that the budget reveals on the part of the government an absolute failure to understand even the elements of those problems which call so loudly for immediate solution. I have been almost inclined to characterize the budget as one of shameless arrogance. When one considers that it has laid heavier burdens upon the people of moderate means, and has absolutely failed to relieve the present widespread distress, in what other light can one regard such a budget? Doctor Randolph Burgess, in his book on the federal reserve system, points out that the proper policy of a central bank is usually to go directly contrary to public opinion. Now, the same policy ought to be adopted by a government in a time of crisis. Private corporations have some excuse for curtailing their expenditures and withholding credit. But the government has adopted a policy of so-called economy, a policy of retrenchment, at the very time when a government ought to extend its expenditures and thus supplement those expenditures that are being made by private individuals and corporations. The government, has coercive powers of taxation, and I submit that it should use the wealth of the nation, now largely held by the few, in the interests of the community at large. I take it that a budget that would meet the needs of to-day would provide for a scaling down of debts, however that can be brought about, whether by means of a direct reduction of debts or through inflation. Further, some form of capital levy should be instituted, because I take it that a comparatively small group of individuals have no right to retain wealth at a time when the great mass of the people are suffering as they are to-day.
My colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) has already called attention to the fact that the Prime Minister made no statement with regard to unemployment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) stated the other day:
This is scarcely the time, just in the spring of the year, for us to be making proposals to the house to deal with unemployment which may be anticipated next autumn. ... The government is thoroughly alive to the situation, is bending every effort to meet it, and in good time will make its proposals known to the house.
I cannot believe that the government is alive to the situation, or it would not allow the budget to pass without a definite announcement regarding its policy on the great question of unemployment. Further than that, the hon. gentleman says that it is no time, in the
spring of the year, to make such proposals. But as we all know, unemployment has been far more prevalent this year, even in the spring, than it has been in any other year, at least so far as my knowledge goes. The spring has gone; this is the summer, and there is every prospect of the situation becoming worse. Yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce actually says that the government will make its policy known in its own good time. Here we are within a few weeks of the close of the session. We have been called from every part of the country to come here for the purpose of dealing with the problems of the nation, and we are told we are not to have an opportunity of discussing any government proposal with respect to this matter. I should like very much to have been able to get through one speech without having to refer to unemployment. But I find it impossible. I am here primarily to represent the labour movement and I cannot avoid bringing to the attention of the house on this occasion the condition as I find it among the labouring classes. The serious distress of the people here in Ottawa is quite manifest. One has only to come in by the Canadian National railways to see what is known as the Ottawa jungle, the place where the tramps and out-of-works gather on the dump heap where they have managed to erect some temporary shelters in which they exist as best they can. Such conditions exist in the capital city of Ottawa. The following editorial appeared in the Montreal Star of June 4:
An immediate crisis faces the city. There are vast numbers of genuine unemployed still walking our streets in dire need. A certain amount of promiscuous, unconeerted aid is being given by charitable organizations and individuals. The Dufferin school was closed in April, but it will soon be necessary to do something to relieve the distress. People cannot be left to starve to death with suicide as the only alternative.
Left to starve with suicide as the only alternative. Do you mean to tell us, Mr. Speaker, that in this country the only alternative to starvation is suicide? There are those who will refuse to accept this alternative. These are the conditions which exist in the city of Montreal, and yet the government tells us that it is alive to the situation and in good time will do something about it. I received a wire the other day from Glace Bay, from which I will read the following sentences:
Whereas the miners at 24 colliery are on the verge of starvation owing to the unemployment at the said colliery working from a day and a half to three days a week and the coal company says they can't give any more employment under present conditions.

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
And later:
Conditions are such that the men are getting out of control and anything is likely to happen.
Evidently these men are not going to accept suicide as the only alternative. Every newspaper -contains information with regard to unemployment. I have a clipping regarding the distress of workers of Abitibi near Sault Ste. Marie, which places have not been referred to this year. A short time ago I attended a meeting in Windsor, called to consider the question of unemployment. I suppose there were fifteen hundred people present and the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand) has drawn attention to the fact that there was considerable disorder. Why? Simply because those people were not content to be told what parliament is doing or what probably would be done by democratic institutions. I would like to pass on to the house a question put to me by one of the men at that meeting. He asked me: What can we do to obtain immediate relief? Only this morning a returned man who was in my office asked me the same question. These men are beginning to get desperate. I have referred already to my own city. On April 10 there were 18,000 unemployed in Winnipeg. According to an editorial which appeared in the Free Press of May 25, it will cost the citizens of Winnipeg this year, irrespective of what has been given by the dominion and provincial authorities, nearly three-quarters of a million dollars to provide relief. The city is almost bankrupt and cannot stand that drain. When we apply to the dominion government they reply: In our own good time. This is the government of which it has been said again and again that it was elected to do away with unemployment. I have a letter from Saskatoon which states that a private citizen is giving out free lunches in addition to the regular work being done. He is doing this simply to help out the boys and to keep down trouble and to bring the plight of these men to the attention of the rulers.
Another newspaper item here from Regina. Unemployment is reaching not only the casual or common labourer but has spread to the skilled mechanic and to the business and professional man. I have advices from Edmonton but I will not take the time of the house to read the details of the desperate situation. A thousand men are being fed with bowls of soup. This is early summer and nothing has been done by the government. Sadder even than the plight of the single man, is that of the married man with a family.

Conditions are not much better out on the prairies. The other day I received a letter from a personal friend of mine, an Englishwoman of good education and high character. She wrote me as follows:
I feel afraid of what another winter may bring; especially if this dry weather and these awful dust storms continue, rain might at least give us food for man and beast. Things are very disheartening for folks who have worked so hard many years. Locally eggs are six cents a dozen, and butter fifteen cents a pound. After investing our earnings in poultry, cattle et cetera, this is what many of us are depending on for ready cash and supplies. We've just had a hard frost which has touched the wheat, nipped any garden stuff that was coming up, and even the tender green leaves of our trees, which have cost us so much to grow, are blackened with the frost.
I received another letter along the same line from a friend in Alberta. There is one sentence which may be of interest to the house, as follows:
Buy feed and sell a five-gallon can of cream for $1.30.
And another:
Eggs are eight cents per dozen, in some places five cents.
Then he refers apparently to an expression of the Prime Minister when he says:
It may be that I do not understand what hardship is. I was born and raised at the west coast of Norway. There we fought the waves for a living from birth to death. I have fought the various drawbacks on the Alberta prairies for almost twenty years now and tried to do my best. ... I am beginning to think that the waves that rocked me while a child and young man were gentle and kind compared with the bumps we receive on the prairie.
When we call attention to these conditions we are called calamity howlers. These quotations show the sufferings of Canadian people, and this government is responsible for not taking action at this time. We are being told that the people must either starve or commit suicide. I wonder! The other day I received from a friend of mine, a parish priest, a copy of an editorial which appeared in the Catholic AVorld of May, 1931, entitled "Starve or Steal?" The opening paragraph read as follows:
AVhen Daniel Willard, president of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad, declared in a recent speech that he would steal rather than starve, some persons and some newspapers considered the statement rather shocking, and novel. Ultra-conservatives possibly called him a bolshevik. But, as all moralists know, the declaration is neither new nor nihilistic. In Catholic ethics, Mr. Willard's daring proposition is a truism.
It is generally contended that the church stands. for the status quo, but I wonder if

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
hon. members have ever taken the trouble to read the sayings of some of the church fathers. Let me give the house a few samples:
St. Basil said:	The bread that you withhold belongs to the hungry.
St. Augustine declared that they who possess superfluities possess the goods of others.
St. Ambrose said:	The earth belongs to
all, not to the rich.
Pope Gregory I wrote:
When we give necessities to the needy, we do not bestow upon them our goods; we return to them their own; we pay a debt of justice rather than of mercy.
And according to St. John Chrysostom, "No one is able to become rich without injustice."
So there is some basis for the statement of Pope Pius:
It is therefore absolutely necessary to reconstruct the whole economic system by bringing it back to the requirements of social justice so as to ensure a more equitable distribution of the united proceeds of capital and labour.
These are not the wild words that are so often considered as desperate in the mouths of agitators against whom we are warned, but the words of those who have been considered the very bulwarks, the very founders of the civilization of western Europe. Yet we are told that the government, in its own good time, will attend to these matters!
Sometimes in the quiet hours I have heard the horses of revolt come galloping, galloping, galloping and I have felt constrained to add the warning of St. James to what I have already given:
Go to, now, ye rich, weep and howl for your miseries that are coming upon you. . . .Ye have laid up great treasure in the last days. . . .Ye have lived delicately on the earth, and taken your pleasure.
I may be told that all this is out of keeping with parliamentary debate, but I feel under a responsibility to represent as best I can the cry of the distressed people of Canada.
What does the budget do under these circumstances? All but the very rich are to be taxed even more heavily and the very rich are to be relieved of a portion of their taxes. The Minister of Trade and Commerce ridicules the amendment which urges the bringing about of a more equitable distribution of the burden of taxation. That, he declares is so old and hoary that no one needs to be worried a particle about it. I ask him: What about his own statement? It strikes me that it is equally old and hoary. He warns us that a tax which drives capital out of the country is on the face of it a bad tax. In that statement there are many assumptions which are far from being true. An economist wrote me the other day:
While it is true that the burden of our income tax must be regulated to some extent by the rate in the United States, it is equally true that the standard of living of our workers must not be very different, if we are to hold our native-born population. If rumours prove correct, the budget is to pay more attention to the emigration of capital than to the emigration of men. No doubt the hoary argument will totter in once more-that the income tax reduces the supply of capital available for domestic industry. This, in spite of the fact that almost twice the proceeds of the tax go right back into the hands of the government's bondholders, 85 per cent of whom are Canadians.
Yes, we are to have very great consideration given to the people of wealth and to the big corporations. I do not think the big corporations have been doing badly in Canada even in this time of stress. We all read a few months ago the annual statement, for example, of the Bank of Montreal which said:
Profits, while reflecting the quiet state, during the past year, of the general business of the country and lower money rates in foreign markets, have been more than sufficient to maintain the usual distributions to shareholders	Rest and undivided profits are
now $2,947,000 in excess of our capital.
Yet these huge corporations are to be very tenderly treated. I come to another big eastern corporation, the Canadian Pacific Railway which has obtained hundreds of millions in money and lands from the people of this country; and yet the president of that great corporation has the assurance to say publicly that he thinks the government should not interfere so much in business. After the corporations have drawn in their hundreds of millions of dollars, from the people, they say: Oh, keep your hands off; we must not be taxed. I want to tell again what we did a year ago, in Winnipeg. We sent a bill to the Canadian Pacific for the amount that the city had had to pay in keeping the unemployed workers of the Canadian Pacific whom, when the spring opened up, they wanted to take back. We could not collect. Yet the corporation resent anything in the way of unemployment insurance or any other measure that might place any burden or responsibility upon them. I do not want to take the time to place on record the figures as to what the Canadian Pacific has received during the years from the people of Canada.
We are told that dividends of Canadian corporations up to $10,000 shall be exempt from taxation to the extent of one-half of the income of the taxpayer. This is another example of how carefully the interests of the big corporations and big taxpayers are being looked after. The. Minister of Trade an\ Commerce warned us of the unfairness of dual taxation, yet on the other hand I need
245S

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
hardly point out that the poorer people pay a triple tax. They pay the tariff; they pay the import tax of one per cent, and then they pay a sales tax of 4 per cent. If I may express my own opinion it is further through their exploitation that the large dividends are created. The whole burden of taxation comes back upon the poorer people. Just let me give a little illustration of how it touches us all. We have been told it was a good thing to have at least a certain amount of fruit and vegetables in our diet. I come from a section of the country where it is impossible to grow most kinds of fruit, where it is impossible to grow early vegetables; it cannot be done. If we want to have these things, we have to pay over and over again for them. Let me give one example. This was even before the heavier taxation was imposed. This is a statement as it appeared in the columns of the Manitoba Free Press a few weeks ago:
A typical case is that of a carload of lettuce which arrived in Winnipeg last week. This came from California. About 300 cases comprised the carload. The particular carload cost $375. The freight charges were $451, a total of $836. And then $968 dumping duty was charged. The duty was, therefore, more than the combined cost of the article itself, and the freight charges from California, an impost of more than 100 per cent on the cost delivered in Winnipeg. On another car, which also came last week, the duty for revenue was $913. Winnipeg consumes aproximatelv four carloads of lettuce a week. Toronto and Montreal would each consume five times as much. It is not difficult to visualize the enormous burden placed on the consumer-without any benefit to the Canadian producer

Because this was weeks before any of the Canadian product had come on the market.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did the hon. member say last week?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; several weeks ago. And I presume the situation is much worse since the new tariff came into operation. I have not the figures.
The Prime Minister is evidently coming to be just a little bit on the defensive. He says:
Can Canada in a protected world be other than a protected country?
I would like to ask another question which I think is much more important: Unless the various countries abandon their so-called protection, can we possibly survive? This is another way of looking at the matter. I should like to read a paragraph from a recent bulletin issued by the Chase National bank of the city of New York. I quote from Benjamin M. Anderson, Junior:
The most serious obstacle in the way of early recovery is the state of our foreign trade. The
[Mr. Woodsworth.l
most serious obstacle in the way of the revival of our foreign trade is our high protective tariffs. The quickest way to get out of the existing depression is to reduce our tariffs so that our foreign customers may sell more goods here and get more dollars with which to pay interest upon their debts to us and with which to buy our goods. If we do not buy we cannot sell. If we do not buy enough we cannot sell enough.
I commend those words, coming from an outsider, a leading economist and banker, to the consideration of the present government. The article goes on-I shall quote only a few sentences:
There are those who would say that it is well enough to reduce the tariffs if all countries will do it, but that no country can do it alone.
That is the position of some. He calls attention to the fact that Holland and Sweden have quietly adhered to their policy of admitting foreign goods without unreasonable restraints and that they are to-day eminently satisfied with the results of their policy. But he warns:
Wages do not depend upon tariffs, and standards of life do not depend upon tariffs. Wages depend upon the productivity of labour per man, and the productivity of labour per man depends, other things being equal, upon the abundance or scarcity of the land and capital with which labour works.
Again:
American labour has nothing to fear and everything to gain, by and large, from a lowering of the tariffs in the United States.
I want to quote a few sentences from an article by William Martin in the Journal de Geneve:
Protection has increased the cost of living and diminished ordinary consumption at the very moment when it was provoking in foreign countries reactions and reprisals and was compromising foreign markets. So that after a brief period of apparent improvement the statesmen in many countries have realized that they were following the wrong path.
Unfortunately they are prisoners of the machine which they have set in motion and which is destroying them. . . .
All the statesmen worthy of that name understand perfectly the remedies which might bring back prosperity to Europe; the unification of the world market or at least a much freer circulation of merchandise. But they feel themselves powerless to apply this remedy; individually, because the resistance of private interests is insurmountable in each country; collectively, because the League of Nations cannot have a determination different from that of its members.
Mr. Martin warns:
If improvement is not brought about, revolution is to be faced. ... If a serious revolution shmdd break out in a great European country it would doubtless only be checked by a war;

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth.
war itself, moreover, would bring about revolution. ... Is a capitalist regime still capable of organizing peace on solid foundations? If the answer is "yes" it will have time to reform its institutions and to assure its future; if the answer is "no" it is condemned to speedy overthrow.
My colleague from North Winnipeg has already called attention to the statement of the manufacturers' association that the policy of the Prime Minister is definitely aimed at making Canada a self-supporting country so far as that is possible. I wish I had time to read a very interesting document recently published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. It contains excellent articles by our own James T. Shotwell and Mr. Raymond B. Fosdick. I will quote a few sentences from Mr. Fosdick. He says:
The solidarity of this new world of ours is the result, of course, of specialization. Each country makes its particular contribution, dependent upon its own resources and capacities, to the goods that the world consumes. It follows, therefore, that no country is self-contained.
He draws the chain of economic consequences as they exist in the world to-day, and I would ask hon. members, if possible, to read this article. He says:
In his recent address before the American Bankers' Association, President Hoover made this rather unguarded comment:
"We are able in considerable degree to free ourselves of world influences and make a large measure of independent recovery because we are so remarkably self-contained."
Mr. Fosdick replies:
A country that could not make a locomotive, an automobile or an airplane without materials from abroad can scarcely be called self-contained. A country that could not even carry on war without the aid of thirty essential commodities from other nations cannot boast of its national independence. By the same token a country whose excess wheat and cotton are rotting in fields and storehouses because its foreign market has gone to pieces is not in a position to talk in terms of Washington's farewell address.
There is the difficulty. We are thinking in terms of an antiquated political and economic regime, and we have not brought up our policies to conform with modern developments.
There is one good thing in the budget, for which I should like to give the government credit, and that is that they are putting on a 2 per cent tax on returns of all investments made by non-residents of this country. They confess that the tax is higher in most other countries, and that the tax here is actually credited to these non-residents in other countries. There is no danger of driving capital
out, of this country. Le<t me give the total investments of outside capital in Canada: Great Britain, $2,197,000,000; United States, $3,470,000,000; rest of the world $237,000,000. Why could we not tax these investments even more heavily? I proposed that last year. I do not know whether the government listened to what I said, but I am glad that they are making a beginning along the lines I suggested. I made another proposal, and that is that we should put a supertax on Canadian capital invested abroad. I am told that one reason why we should be so careful not to tax too heavily the very large incomes is that otherwise capital might migrate from this country. There is a great deal easier and far more effective way of keeping it here, and that is to put a supertax on all of it that goes abroad. If the government is really in earnest about having business retained in Canada, let them keep Canadian capital in Canada. I am not putting this forward as my own position, because I think that policy along these lines is all nonsense, but I say that if the government is in earnest about its policy, that is what should be done.
Let me give figures as to the amount of Canadian investments abroad. They are two years old, but the latest available from the bureau of statistics. They show that in Great Britain there are Canadian investments to the amount, $96,000,000; in the United States, $992,000,000; in the rest of the world, $65S,-000,000. Why not bring that Canadian capital home by taxing it, and taxing it until it does come home? But again I warn that it is absolute nonsense to pay so much attention to these international lines.
One of the speakers on the other side tonight spoke of some American firm building or proposing to build a factory in this country on the assurance that the government would carry out its promise to protect Canadian industires. It all seems so absolutely ridiculous. There are 1,500 branches of American industries established in Canada. A recent Canadian Pacific Railway bulletin actually listed some 1,150 of these branches. It- is very interesting to note that a great many of them carry the name "Canadian" or "Dominion". They are very anxious to be known as Canadian or Dominion companies, but they are essentially American industries, and the profits of these industries are going over to the other side of the line. These industries come over here very largely because wages here have been lower than they have been in the United States, not because wages here are higher.

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
I should like to have had time to call fuller attention to the fact that although there is so much hardship among a great many wage earners and the people generally in this country, the big companies have not been doing so badly. Just the other day I noticed this statement in one of our Canadian papers:
Despite reductions and omissions in the dividends paid by Canadian corporations, distributions to be made in the month of June will reach the large total of $27,467,187.
It does not look as though the big corporations were going bankrupt. We are in line in this as in other matters with the trends in the United States. I noticed that in 1930 the net profits of some nine hundred industrial corporations in the United States amounted to $2,097,823,000. The capital and surplus amounted to $28,929,975,000. The rate of return for 'the year 1930 was 7.2 per cent. Any government which really represented the interests of the people would see to it that a very considerable proportion of those big dividends were transferred from private people to meet the present, needs of the general community of this country.
In the few minutes which remain to me I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the income tax. In the year 1929, according to figures I have been able to procure, the amount of income assessed for purposes of income tax totalled SI,195,402,266. I notice that the vast majority of the people in this country do not earn enough money to pay income tax. Those earning under $2,000 numbered onbr 36,857 and paid a total tax of only $341,777. Farther down in the table before me I find that 523 people received an income of $50,000 per year and over. The total tax paid by them was $9,328,921. Coming to the corporation taxes I find that 1,181 corporations paid a total tax of $30,410,897. To the table showing taxes paid by corporations there is added the following footnote:
Totals include 7 corporations paying $18,007 in taxation, grouped to conceal net income and identity of taxpayers.
That footnote to my mind is most extraordinary. The fact is worthy of comment that even in our official figures there is an arrangement made so as to conceal the identity of large income taxpayers and the amounts paid by them. That principle to my mind is wrong. We are told this country belongs to the people, and yet when we came to matters of taxation we find the taxes are loaded upon only a few people. What are the great majority of these taxes collected for? They are collected so that we may turn them over to those people who during

or since the war managed to secure, a mortgage on the country. I have often thought that this government is nothing more or less than a vast debt collecting agency operating to collect from the poor people or the people of moderate means moneys to be turned over to the wealthy people. We are making provision not only to enable these wealthy people to retain their wealth but to enable them to secure more wealth.
I wish I had time to go into the moral side of this question, but I am afraid that upon this occasion, I cannot do so. In the earlier part of my address I ventured to quote from eminent authorities who had made statements regarding the moral issues involved. I think the time has come about when we shall have to definitely challenge the right of the rich to hold money in their possession at a time when other people are suffering.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to say a few words on the amendment and also to make a few comments with respect to the budget. I shall direct my remarks more particularly to the conditions of distress and unemployment which prevail at the present time. I must say I was somewhat disappointed when no relief measures were mentioned in the budget, and I was further disappointed in the knowledge that greater burdens have been placed upon the shoulders of the Canadian people through the recent changes brought down by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I was particularly pleased with the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) because I believe he touched upon matters which since the beginning of the session have not been discussed as fully as they might have been.
Before passing on to my remarks concerning the unemployment situation I should like to say a few words regarding the remarks of my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) concerning the Canadian National Railways. I do not intend to go very fully into the figures, but I for one feel that the ill-timed remarks of the hon. member with respect to the Canadian National Railways should not be allowed to go unchallenged. I am sorry the hon. member is not in his seat, because I wished particularly to remind him that as a lawyer he ought to know there are always two sides to a question.. One side has been ably presented by my hon. friend,

The Budget

and I shall attempt to present the other side. I should like to remind him when he talks about public ownership as opposed to private ownership, and about the position of the Canadian Pacific Railway as a business concern opposed to the position of the Canadian National Railways-
