speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the interest my hon. friends opposite are taking shows that I have hit upon a popular subject. All hon. members will recall the arrogant attitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway employees in (he day when there was only one large railway in Canada. We were told in those days where we had to market our beef and our other products. Cars were held up for weeks and our stock could not be shipped owing to the fact that there was only one railroad. But what do we have to-day? When we go to the Canadian Pacific Railway it is, "Yes, sir," and "Yes, please," and so on. The different attitude now taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway officials is due entirely to the competition offered by the government owned Canadian National Railways.
As one of the new members, here for the first year, and one who has listened attentively to practically every speech made since parliament opened, I must say that it sounded just a little strange to me when I listened to hon. members opposite who, when the distress of the common people was being referred to, stated, and oftentimes shoulted across the floor of the house, "What did the Liberal party do during the last nine years?" Well, Mr. Speaker, if the Liberal party did not realize the gravity of the economic distress last year, and did not take steps such as the right hon. Prime Minister said they ought to have taken, more especially as he himself has said he had warned them of what was coming; if, as has been said, the Liberal party was at fault-and I am not quite prepared to admit that-what shall the condemnation be of the present administration who, prophesying all the calamities now in existence as the result of the rule of the Liberal party, and who, with unemployment greater now than at any period in our history, knowing also that the general distress of the people is very great indeed in some parts of Canada, if not throughout the whole of our country; knowing as I say all these matters, what shall be said of the present administration who, to quote scripture, when the people cried for bread, gave them a stone? Because, Mr. Speaker, I find nothing in the budget to help the masses of our people who are in want to-day, and who, in their distress have been looking to the government as never before, for some measure of assistance.
Many times in this house, quotations of the right hon. Prime Minister's speeches which he made during the election of last year, have been cited regarding some of the promises made to the people of this country, especially with regard to unemployment. I would just like to point out at this time, Mr. Speaker, the very seriousness of all such promises made to the people of Canada and to point out to hon. members the seriousness of all utterances and promises made on the public platform by either the Prime Minister or by whoever happens to be leader of the opposition. The-average member of parliament or the average person running for office may at times make rash promises which perhaps are only applicable to the local districts concerned. But the utterances or promises of the Prime Minister or of the leader of the opposition are taken much more seriously by the people as a whole because they speak as it were with some authority. When the country is in a fairly prosperous condition such promises are easily and oftentimes forgotten and are not taken as seriously as I
The Budget-Mr. Reid

believe they should be. But, when the nation is in a distressed condition, when thousands are seeking work and many persons have no food or clothing or shelter of any kind, and when the great majority of fanners are also in distress and in need, the promises of either the Prime Minister or of the leader of the opposition are taken very literally by the people, and they expect that any promises so made will be carried out. There is absolutely no doubt that thousands of people throughout Canada were looking for someone who would at least help them in their serious difficulties, and so when the present Prime Minister and others of his government spoke from one end of Canada to the other in no uncertain language saying, "We will end unemployment''1-"work for every ablebodied man and woman who wants to work."-the people throughout Canada accepted those plain statements as a solution of their trouble. Here was at last someone or some party who would remedy their economic ills.
Hon. members opposite say, "Oh, we did not intend to end unemployment in eight months or even in one year. Give us time." But, Mr. Speaker, the people throughout this country accepted literally the very definite words of the Prime Minister and others and fully expected that he would accomplish what he and they said they would do, namely, end unemployment, now-not next year, or the year after, but if and when elected. That was the understanding of the people of this country, that was the way they understood the utterances, and the Prime Minister's words were so definite and so plain that at the time they were spoken no one was in any doubt as to their meaning. However, Mr. Speaker, there does exist no doubt now in the minds of the common people as to what he meant; they know now that those promises meant less than nothing. And the bitterness and disappointment felt by many of those who are to-day in terrible financial straits and in poverty can best be realized by those of us who have daily dealings with the farmers and the workers, or with those who would be glad to work if only work could be given them. I believe that a very grievous injustice has been imposed on the people by such utterances and the failure to fulfil those promises, and that failure has had far reaching effects on the morale of the people of this country since the election of last year.
The confidence of the common people in the rulers of this country has been shaken

to an extent never before realized in the history of Canada, and I have no hesitation in stating, Mr. Speaker, that the idle promises made to the unemployed and to the farmers of this country by the Prime Minister which promises in large measure gained them control or power, have had far more serious effect on the minds and the morale of many people throughout Canada than any socialist propaganda could possibly have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been repeatedly stated by members to your right that no solution has been offered by hon. members on this side. I may state that very many suggestions have been made by hon. members from this side of the house, but it would seem that any suggestions so made fall on deaf ears. I believe that the right hon. the Prime Minister would have been well advised to study some of the methods adopted by countries such as Great Britain. The laws enacted in that country have had the effect of directly distributing her wealth more evenly amongst the forty some odd million people, without impoverishing the resources or the great wealth of the country.
The British government went after the wealthy millionaires, taking the bulk of the taxes from those that had the greater surplus of wealth. The right hon. Prime Minister, however, has taken a very different method. By the budget recently brought down his policy is to tax the masses more than ever, and allow the very wealthy to get still wealthier. We have in this country great wealth, wonderful natural resources and plenty for all, but it is held in the hands of too few of our people.
In the new budget and one which he says himself had been the only budget brought down in a great number of years, the bulk of taxation is most certainly placed on those least able to bear it, and the money barons, amongst whose numbers members of the present government I believe, can be counted, and who, Mr. Speaker, are in a class by themselves-these have been relieved to some extent of the taxes they formerly paid, and which had been imposed on them by the Liberal party, and which I maintain they could very well afford to pay out of the abundance of the wealth they have and control. The Conservative party is certainly running true to form; the very wealthy, it seems, must be protected. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to read you something to show what they have done with millionaires in Great Britain-and in passing I would observe that no country has been such a bulwark against what is termed bolshevism or against revolution as the mother country has been; that land where such things as free speech and unemployment insurance, coupled also with the taking of the surplus wealth from the millionaires and giving it back to the people, have done a great deal to maintain the country in the wonderful position in which we find it to-day. And that, after passing through the terrible conditions of the war, with its after effects. The mother country has always taken an interest in the welfare of the masses.
The article from vrhich I am going to quote appeared in the Vancouver Province of March 29 and reads thus:
Millionaires are fast dying out in British Isles. High taxation, reducing numbers at rate of nearly two a month.
London, March 28.-Twenty-five years hence, a wealthy Britou-the kind of man who can write you a cheque for a million pounds-will be world-famous whether he wishes it or not. He will be the last millionaire in the country. Enormously rich men are fast dying out in the British Isles, so rapidly are they losing their great possessions at the hands of those grim despoilers, who have their dens in the
inland revenue departments	However,
the national wealth is still growing in spite of the decline of the super-rich. There are 50,000 more income taxpayers now than there -were a year ago. Taxation may be redistributing wealth, but it does not seem to be diminishing it. Still, even yet, there is a wonderful concentration of money and its equivalents in the hands of a very small group of people in Britain.
In that country, Mr. Speaker, a man is termed a millionaire if he has over $250,000 a year; and a man with an income of $750,000 contributes $350,000 of that amount to the state. Yet the mother country is a land we are all proud of. As I say, it has been the great bulwark against revolution. I say therefore that it is about time that we in this country learned a lesson from the motherland.
I observed, Mr. Speaker, that while in his speech the Prime Minister assumed responsibility for the various measures brought down in the budget, he did not do so with respect to the changes introduced in the new income tax schedule. When, in his address, he came to the income tax changes the Prime Minister quoted the findings of Mr. Walters, saying, "We adopted his findings." Well, no wonder
The Budget-Mr. Reid

the Prime Minister hesitated in this connection, for by the changes that have been introduced the money barons of this country will be saved large sums. I just wonder what representations they made to gain that relief. I honestly believe that if ever there was a time when the millionaires should be forced to give up a part of their great surplus wealth that time is the present. I do not say all their wealth, because I do not believe in an equal distribution to all men. I do say, however, that this it a time when they should give up some of their great surplus, and I believe they will have ultimately to be gouged out of it. They will have to give part of it back to the state. In the midst of this economic blizzard we are passing through, this would have been the time for the government to have gone a long way in that direction. But as the Prime Minister said at page 2171 of Hansard, the taxes imposed should be those with which the people are most familiar. Yes, the people have been very familiar with taxes of this kind. After all, Mr. Speaker, should not the workers of the country, the people who have helped in large measure to build up this dominion, participate to a greater extent in the great wealth which they have been instrumental in creating? I believe I am safe in saying, as has been said by many before me, that without land and without labour no wealth is possible.
Let me quote from the Prime Minister's peroration with respect to the Pilgrim Fathers. The right hon. gentleman said in part:
Will not a few idle drones spoil the whole stock of laborious bees? So one idle belly, one murmurer, one complainer, one self-lover, will weaken and dishearten a whole colony. Great matters have been brought to pass, where men have cheerfully, as with one heart, hand and shoulder, gone about it, both in wars, buildings and plantations; but where every man seeks himself, all eometh to nothing.
I wonder whether the Prime Minister really believed these fine Chronicles of the Pilgrim Fathers. I am somewhat afraid they were empty words; because if he was sincere he would certainly not have placed the burden of taxation on those least able to bear it, without first of all going after those wealthy barons to whom I have been referring. Members of the Conservative party have protested that they must have time to solve many of the problems involved in the promises they made during the last election. Well, the greatest problem, and the most serious one, has not yet even been mentioned. The Prime Minister said that the government would end unemployment or perish in the attempt. I am afraid it is the people who are going to

perish in the attempt. The Conservative party seems to have done fairly well so far. Employment is increasing every day.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unemployment, rather. Yes,
I know hon. gentlemen opposite would like me to say that intentionally. And, Mr. Speaker, I should certainly be glad to be able to make such a statement truthfully.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the truth will out.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You will get the truth in regard to unemployment in a few moments if you wait. Unemployment is increasing every day. This is almost the middle of the year and many cities and municipalities are at the present moment looking after hundreds of unemployed, preparing in advance to take care of those within their own borders who are likely to be up against it this winter. They have given out that only transients will be taken care of this winter owing to the fact that their resources are gone. Soup kitchens are being advocated, and many cities and municipalities intend to provide only for those who have been resident twelve months or more, so great has been the burden during the past year.
The Prime Minister called a special session last year in an endeavour to deal with the situation', and many hon. members would have us believe that something wonderful has been accomplished. While I am free to admit that had not the offer been available last winter to contribute 25 cents for every dollar spent by the municipalities, conditions would have been worse. The fact remains however that every city and municipality was forced' to borrow on future tax payments if it wanted to take advantage of that offer. Every city and municipality, in British Columbia at least, went into debt by so doing, and necessary works have had to be curtailed this year by reason of that borrowing. And, Mr. Speaker, if the same offer were made this fall-and at the present moment unemployment is quite serious and is likely to be worse this fall and winter-no city or municipality would be in a position to avail itself of that offer. It will be all that the cities and municipalities can do to provide for their usual expenditures. The government will have, to step in and provide the funds necessary and now is the time when ways and means should be discussed as to the best method to pursue and the various works and projects which should be carried on. This parliament should not prorogue without putting into effect some

The Budget-Mr. Reid
scheme to alleviate both now and this coming winter the suffering which is facing this country.
In regard to unemployment the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said: We are aware of it, and before the session ends some announcement will be made. He mentioned something about its not being a good thing to speak about this matter on account of the effect upon the morale of the people. We should not be afraid to grapple with this situation; no good will come if we refuse to meet it honestly and openly. Cities and municipalities along with public and charitable organizations cannot cope with this social disease which to my mind is almost as serious to-day as was the late war.
The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce quoted some figures to show that unemployment to-day is just as favourable as it was some years ago. However that may be, the fact remains that the figures furnished by the government show that unemployment .has increased, especially in British Columbia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And everywhere.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unemployment is certainly
more prevalent to-day than it was last fall and it is increasing month by month.
I would like to quote from correspondence and some cuttings which have been sent to me and which refer to this serious situation. The first article is from Vernon, British Columbia, and is headed, "Bishop Urges Clergy to Investigate Conditions Cities' Jungles." Surely no hon. member will accuse this body of being partisan. The next communication is from Burnaby and is to the effect that its unemployed list has increased 25 per cent during May over the April figures. The situation is growing worse and they have no funds left for unemployment relief. The article continues:
The reeve submitted correspondence with Hon. Gideon Robertson, Minister of Labour, who stated that while relief of destitute was primarily a municipal responsibility, the government had set up a fund to assist municipalities with direct relief. But, the minister said, the fund for unemployment relief is exhausted.
I could quote many other reports from other municipalities, but at this time I do not intend to go deeply into this matter. The government of British Columbia sent out notices to the various municipalities asking if they wished to participate in the relief funds. Many municipalities sent back the reply that they were unable to take advantage of any offer in connection with which they would be called upon to contribute any money. I would direct the attention of the house to a letter which I received this morning from a 22110-157
gentleman at Aleza Lake. He wants to know how it will be possible for him to live on the wages he is receiving. This man is being paid 20 cents per hour for a nine hour day, six days per week. He draws $10.80 per week, out of which the company takes $8.81 for board. He has $1.99 per week left to send to his wife for the support of his family.
I am of the opinion that many hon. members do not fully realize the gravity of the situation. Unemployment stalks throughout the land, not only in this country but in nearly all countries of the world. Ways and means should be considered from a much wider national point of view and with the object of so changing our whole social and economic system as to cope with affairs as we find them to-day and endeavour to alleviate the sufferings of our people so as to preserve this great country from action which might be called revolutionary. It is my belief that not only is the wealth of the country in the hands of the very few to the detriment of the masses, but the hours of work should be distributed-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has
spoken many times in this house of the great courage and loyalty inherent in the Canadian people. I submit that never was that courage more strongly exemplified and that loyalty shown to greater advantage than during the past ten or twelve months. I am of the opinion that had our ten millions of people been in one province only, conditions would be much more serious than they are to-day. The fact that Canada is three thousand miles across has helped to alleviate conditions.
I will touch briefly upon the tariff, more especially in connection with the one per cent impost and the three per cent increase in the sales tax. I do not believe in the policy of attempting to have Canada live and trade within herself. That is not a sound or

The Budget-Mr. Reid

sane policy; no country can tax itself rich. A nation is similar to a person; no country can live unto itself and prosper, and neither can a person. I believe that the putting up of tariff walls is a bad policy, and if persisted in by nations will lead ultimately to war. This country should not erect a high tariff wall simply because other countries have done so. There are those who would like us to trade with Russia, while others are in favour of a complete stoppage of trade. I believe it was unwise to attempt to fight Russia economically. By that move Canada has been left high and dry in her righteousness, and it would be a brave man who would point the finger of scorn at the motherland or any other country for being wise enough to trade with Russia.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has spoken about the duty on coal, and for a moment I will discuss this particular matter. It may be that the duty on coal has been increased in order to help out certain provinces, such as Nova Scotia, but I can assure the house that the province of British Columbia is receiving no benefit. The following is a report which appeared in the Vancouver Province of May 31:
Premier Tolmie to-day put himself on record as definitely opposed to duties on bituminous coal imported into Canada. In a telegram to the federal government, he said this province would suffer from such duties which, according to Ottawa despatches, may be included in the Bennett budget on Monday. The Premier said that from what he had heard in Ottawa himself he was not at all certain that coal duties would be included in the budget, but in case any such plan is under %vay, he wants this province's views to be known in advance. He explained that a duty on American coal would be almost sure to bring retaliation from the United States, which would shut Crowsnest pass coal out of the American market and seriously damage British Columbia coal mining. "This," the Premier said, "would be a serious blow to us."
In connection with the question of coal, I should like to draw the attention of the government to the fact that Colonel Villiers says that many thousand tons of coal are entering British Columbia ports as lignite free of duty; on tests being made they are found to be bituminous and are sent out from United States points listed as subbituminous, but when they come to this country they are classified here as lignite and so enter free.

Does the hon. member
object to the duty that was provided by the budget on lignite coal?

If there is a duty on lignite
entering Canada, I accept that statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but Colonel Villiers, speaking for the coal industry in British Columbia, said just the other day that this coal was coming in free as lignite.

speechtext:
It has been coming in
free. We have now put a duty on lignite as well as on anthracite. I asked the hon. member:	Does he object to that duty being
imposed on lignite?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No. I have doubts as to just what effect the proposed payment of five cents a bushel to the farmer on export wheat will have. I sincerely hope it will be of great help to them, but I am not sure that it will not mean more to the railway companies and to the buyers of wheat in foreign countries than to the Canadian farmers generally. We in British Columbia, instead of receiving any such help, have been further penalized to the extent of a 25 cents per bushel tax on corn from Argentina or elsewhere. Had the growers of barley been given a bonus of five cents a bushel or more on all barley shipped out of their province, or had the purchasers of grain in British Columbia been given a bonus as they should have been, in view of the exorbitant freight rates we have to pay for olir domestic supplies, we in that province could have enjoyed this with the same fervour as the wheat farmers in the prairie provinces are enjoying it, if they are doing so. But it seems that what I have previously stated is only too true: British Columbia appears to be too far away from Ottawa. It will certainly be a blow to our farmers in British Columbia when they are called upon to pay this extra 25 cents a bushel on the corn which is a very necessary part of the ration used on all farms.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Can they not use a little barley in place of corn?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I have time, I shall be glad to go into that question, because it is evident the hon. member was never in the poultry business or he would not ask the question. I believe that some 35,000 bushels of corn entered British Columbia last year. Corn is a very necessary article. Barley has been discussed in the house, but those who argue that barley is just as good as corn as a poultry diet are evidently office farmers; they are not practical farmers. Poultrymen in British Columbia are not accustomed to using barley; they have always preferred corn because it is more palatable and in past years it has been much cheaper than barley on account of the high freight rates on barley from the prairie

Beauharnois Power Corporation
provinces. This tax of 25 cents per bushel on corn which the poultrymen will be called upon to pay will be prohibitive. This is a fine gesture after the goodwill mission that we sent down to Argentina not so long ago. It will block this channel of trade that has been nmning between the two countries.
